# Project Learnings — vscode-quarto-ext

**What this is:** the append-only table of project-specific learnings accumulated at each
session's Phase 3C close-out (`SESSION_RUNNER.md` §3C). Extracted here from `CLAUDE.md` on
2026-07-09 (Session 39) because the table had grown to ~97% of that file's size (159 KB of
164 KB, 45 rows) and `CLAUDE.md` is loaded in full into every session's context — this file
is not. `CLAUDE.md` → Project-Specific Methodology Adaptations → Project-specific Learnings
now carries a plain Markdown link pointer to this file (deliberately not an `@`-import, which
would auto-expand into context every session and defeat the purpose of moving this out).

**This file is project-owned** — committed at the project root like `CLAUDE.md` itself, never
touched by `bin/sync` (that only touches `SESSION_RUNNER.md`, `SAFEGUARDS.md`,
`docs/methodology/**`, and other byte-identical canonical copies). No tooling changes were
needed to adopt it.

**How to use it:**
- **At Phase 3C (Document Learnings):** append a new row to the bottom of the table below with
  the next sequential number. Do not add rows back to `CLAUDE.md`.
- **At Phase 0 / when starting work in a previously-touched area:** grep this file for relevant
  keywords (a phase name, a file path, a feature name) rather than reading it in full — it will
  keep growing, exactly as it did inside `CLAUDE.md`.

| # | Learning | When to apply |
|---|----------|---------------|
| 1 | **Posit's official Quarto VS Code extension is AGPL-3.0** (extension, LSP, Visual Editor, Panmirror — confirmed twice against the live `quarto-dev/quarto` repo). It is **look-but-don't-copy** reference only. Build on MIT upstreams instead: `microsoft/vscode-markdown-tm-grammar`, `wooorm/markdown-tm-language`, `microsoft/vscode-markdown-languageservice`, and the MIT Quarto **CLI** (shelled out at runtime). | Before reusing/adapting any Quarto-extension code, or choosing a grammar/LSP base. The MIT boundary in CONTEXT.md is non-negotiable. |
| 2 | **Language-support architecture is resolved: ship Tier A (TextMate grammar) → build to Tier B (in-process `register*Provider`) → defer Tier C (out-of-process LSP).** The guardrail that makes this safe: the intelligence core is a **`vscode`-free pure-TS library**; the extension is a thin adapter. This makes B→C migration cheap AND makes the core unit-testable headlessly. See `docs/planning/2026-06-27-extension-architecture-plan.md` §3. | Any language-feature work. Keep parsing/analysis logic out of `vscode.*` imports. |
| 3 | **Automated runtime verification WORKS here — `@vscode/test-electron` confirmed in Phase 1 (Session 2).** Despite no `code` CLI on PATH, test-electron downloads its own VS Code (v1.126.0, ~261 MB into `.vscode-test/`, gitignored) and runs integration tests **headlessly**: it activates the extension in a real host and executes commands end-to-end (Phase 1's test runs `quarto.verifyInstallation` against the real CLI, exit 0). This is **stronger than manual F5** for wiring/activation/dispatch. Manual F5 remains the only way to visually confirm notification/UI text. Pure-`core/` logic is unit-tested with `npm test` (vitest, no VS Code). | Phase 3E for any implementation session: prefer `npm run test:integration` for runtime-behavior verification; reserve manual F5 for visual/UX confirmation. Never claim build-clean == runtime-clean — but you can now usually *prove* runtime-clean automatically. |
| 4 | **Verified Quarto CLI behaviors (trust these):** `quarto --version` prints just the bare semver (`1.7.33\n`, no banner); `quarto preview <f>` prints `Browse at http://localhost:<port>/` (parse this for the preview webview); `--timeout` does NOT reliably self-exit (only on no active clients → own the process lifecycle, kill on close); code-cell render needs Jupyter (`nbformat`) in the active Python env. | Phases 3–5 (render/preview/execution). Re-verify the `Browse at` line on Quarto CLI upgrades. |
| 5 | **Phase 1 build toolchain (working — trust these).** Two compilers by design: esbuild bundles `src/extension.ts` → `dist/extension.js` (`vscode` external); a SEPARATE `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` compiles `test/integration/**` → `out/` for test-electron to run. vitest is scoped to `test/unit/**` so it never picks up the mocha integration tests. **Gotchas caught in Phase 1:** `.vscodeignore` MUST exclude `.claude/**` and `.git/**` (else they leak into the `.vsix`); `npm run package` needs `--allow-missing-repository` and README must avoid relative links (e.g. `./LICENSE`) until a git remote + `repository` field exist. | Any session that compiles/tests/packages. When a git remote is added: drop `--allow-missing-repository`, add `repository` to package.json, and the README relative-link restriction lifts. |
| 6 | **Phase 2 grammar — base-grammar question RESOLVED by NOT forking.** `syntaxes/quarto.tmLanguage.json` (scope `text.html.quarto`) is **original work** that `include`s VS Code's built-in `text.html.markdown` **by scope-name reference** (no source copied) for prose/plain fences, and adds only the Quarto-specific rules: a `\A`-anchored YAML front-matter region (→`source.yaml`) and brace-cell rules ` ```{python|r|julia|ojs} ` (→`source.python`/`source.r`/`source.julia`/`source.js`). This beats forking `markdown-tm-language`/`vscode-markdown-tm-grammar` (nothing large to copy/attribute; markdown stays current) and is the canonical `mjbvz` injection pattern (MIT). Each cell's content is `contentName: meta.embedded.block.<lang>`, mapped to a language in `package.json` → `contributes.grammars.embeddedLanguages` (this mapping, not the grammar, is what enables bracket-match/comment-toggle inside cells). A `cell-generic` fallback scopes any other `{lang}`. **Caveat:** `source.r`/`source.julia` are NOT bundled with VS Code — those cells get the fenced + `meta.embedded.block.*` scope but only colorize if the user has the R/Julia extension installed (python/js always colorize). Attribution is in `/NOTICE` (licensing hard gate). | Any grammar/highlighting work, or adding a new cell language (add a `cell-<lang>` rule + an `embeddedLanguages` entry + a `tokenize.test.ts` assertion). |
| 7 | **Headless grammar verification works — automate token scopes, don't defer to F5.** `test/unit/tokenize.test.ts` loads the grammar into the SAME engines VS Code uses (`vscode-textmate` + `vscode-oniguruma`, both MIT devDeps) and tokenizes the fixture, asserting `meta.embedded.block.*` scopes + the discriminating cases (a plain ` ```python ` block and post-cell prose must NOT be in a cell). This is the automated equivalent of "Developer: Inspect Editor Tokens and Scopes" and catches regex bugs (back-referenced closing fence, `\A` anchor, `\b` boundaries) the structural JSON guard cannot. **Load-bearing gotcha:** in the standalone test registry, `loadGrammar` MUST return an empty stub `{scopeName, patterns: []}` for unresolved external includes (markdown/yaml/source.*), **NOT `null`** — returning null silently corrupts vscode-textmate's pattern compilation (sibling rules stop matching / reorder), which cost most of Phase 2's debugging. Real VS Code always has those grammars, so the extension itself is unaffected. **Fixture trick:** `#| eval: false` on `{python}`/`{r}`/`{julia}` cells lets `quarto render` validate the doc (exit 0) WITHOUT needing Jupyter/R/Julia kernels. | Verifying any grammar (prefer this over manual F5 for scopes — extends Learning #3; F5 remains only for theme-dependent COLOR). Writing render-clean `.qmd` fixtures (Phases 3/5). |
| 8 | **`quarto render` I/O contract (verified live 1.7.33 — extends Learning #4).** Progress, the `Output created: <path>` success marker, AND error text all go to **STDERR**; STDOUT is empty. So you CANNOT distinguish success from failure by stream — **key off the exit code** (0 = success, non-zero = failure; missing-Jupyter is exit 1 with the `nbformat` traceback verbatim on stderr). The reported output path is **relative to the input file's directory** (resolve against `dirname(file)`), and the marker line may be wrapped in **ANSI SGR escapes** (`\x1b[..m`) — strip them before parsing. Stream BOTH stdout+stderr to the Output channel; `core/render-args.ts` keeps `buildRenderArgs` + `parseOutputPath` pure/testable. | Phase 4 preview (also parses a stderr line — `Browse at`), Phase 5 execution, or any CLI-wrapper feature. Capture the real stream layout live before coding the parser. |
| 9 | **Faithful-verification trap in the test-electron host (gate d / FM #24): the host resolves a DIFFERENT Python than your interactive shell.** Phase 3's missing-Jupyter fixture (`needs-jupyter.qmd`, executable `{python}`, no `eval:false`) **fails via the CLI in this shell** (miniforge python, no `nbformat`) but **renders SUCCESSFULLY inside the downloaded VS Code host** (it resolves a Jupyter-capable python). An `assert.doesNotReject` failure-path test against it therefore passes **trivially** (a success also doesn't reject) — verifying nothing. Fix: for automated failure-path tests use an **environment-independent deterministic failure** (`render-error.qmd`: an invalid `format:` → exit 1 "Validation of YAML front matter failed" in ANY env, no kernel) and verify env-dependent degradation (missing Jupyter) **live via the CLI**. **Timing is a faithfulness signal:** the genuine failure runs in <1s; a sneaky success runs in ~4s (kernel+pandoc). | Phase 5 run-cell and any test of a degradation/error path whose trigger depends on the host environment (kernels, installed extensions, PATH). Don't trust a green "does-not-throw" test unless the failure it claims to exercise is environment-independent. |
| 10 | **Strict TDD is mandatory project-wide (operator directive, Session 5).** Every implementation/bug-fix task follows red → green → refactor, one test at a time, vertical slices (never all-tests-then-all-code). The binding statement and exact scope/exemptions are in the **§"Mandatory development practice — strict TDD"** subsection above; the `/tdd` skill is the operative how-to. | Start of any implementation/bugfix session — invoke `/tdd` and write the failing test before the code. Pure config/grammar/doc edits with no logic are exempt but still need their normal verification. |
| 11 | **`quarto preview` process-tree reaping + the deno-worker faithful-verification trap (Phase 4, verified live 1.7.33).** `quarto preview` is a **bash wrapper** (`/usr/local/bin/quarto preview …`) that spawns a long-lived **deno worker** whose cmdline reads **`…deno run … quarto.js preview …`**. Two load-bearing consequences: (a) **Killing the wrapper first REPARENTS the deno worker** (it survives, orphaned) — so spawn **`detached: true`** (the wrapper leads a process group) and signal the whole group atomically: `process.kill(-pid, "SIGTERM")` then, gated on a `process.kill(-pid, 0)` liveness probe, `"SIGKILL"`. A group outlives its leader while any member is alive, so the group signal still reaps a wrapper-died/worker-alive case. (b) **`pgrep -f "quarto preview"` matches the wrapper but NOT the deno worker** (`quarto.js preview` ≠ `quarto preview`) — so a `"quarto preview"` probe/`pkill` reports "clean" while the deno worker orphans (a gate-d trap; it bit my own capture script AND would have made the no-orphan test pass falsely). Use a fixture-scoped pattern that matches **both**: `pgrep -f "preview.*<fixture>"`. The `Browse at <url>` marker is on **STDERR** (stdout empty), ANSI-wrapped — Learning #8 extends to preview; pin the live-captured line. | Phase 5+ or any long-lived-CLI feature: spawn detached, group-kill, and write the no-orphan probe to match the real worker process, not the wrapper. Re-verify the wrapper/worker topology on a Quarto upgrade. |
| 12 | **Long-lived-process managers have check-then-act races across `await`s — and an adversarial review caught one the integration test missed (Phase 4).** The "one preview per document" guard read the sessions map, but the session was only registered **after** two awaits (`doc.save()`, `resolveBinary()` — which spawns `quarto --version`, uncached). Two rapid `quarto.preview` invocations both passed the guard and both spawned; the second's session overwrote the first in the map, so the first server was tracked by nothing and **orphaned permanently (surviving deactivate)** — defeating the whole no-orphan design. Fix: **reserve the slot synchronously in a `Set` before the first await** (try/finally to release). The single-invocation integration test was green and missed it; a 4-lens adversarial review (with adversarial verification of each finding) surfaced it + 4 lower-severity issues. Lesson: for any in-process manager keyed by an id, make check-and-claim atomic *before* the first await; and run an adversarial review over lifecycle/concurrency code — a passing happy-path test is not coverage of the race. | Any feature that tracks long-lived resources in a map/registry across async setup (Phase 5 run-cell sessions, future preview-format/port features). Reserve the key synchronously; add a concurrent-invocation regression test. |
| 13 | **Phase 5 delegated run-cell — three load-bearing facts (one a dead-on-arrival bug the integration suite masked).** (a) **`activationEvents: []` does NOT activate the extension when a `.qmd` is opened** — `contributes.languages`/`grammars` do not trigger activation; only the auto-generated `onCommand` does. So a keybinding gated on a context key the extension sets in `activate()` (here `quarto.inCodeCell`, gating `ctrl/shift+enter`) is **dead until the user first runs a palette command**. Fix: add **`onLanguage:quarto`** to `activationEvents`. The integration suite force-`activate()`s the extension in its `before()` hook, so it **masked** this — an adversarial review caught it; a real fresh-open (F5) or a `packageJSON.activationEvents` contribution-guard test is needed. (b) **Faithful delegated-dispatch testing = register a STAND-IN delegate command.** The clean `@vscode/test-electron` host has no Jupyter, so `vscode.commands.registerCommand("jupyter.execSelectionInteractive", …)` is free; have the stand-in capture the **selected text** at call time to prove the full chain (find-cell → select-code → invoke-delegate) and pin the selection math, env-independently (gate d; extends Learning #9). (c) **Run-cell runs the IN-EDITOR buffer (no `doc.save()`)** — unlike render/preview, which save because the CLI reads from disk; the delegated path's dependency is the user's **kernel + language extension**, not the Quarto CLI (distinct from Learning #4/#9's render-path Jupyter need). | Any feature gated on an extension-set context key, or expected to work on file-open before any command runs (→ add `onLanguage:`, and don't trust a suite that force-activates); testing any feature that delegates to an external command ID (→ stand-in command + assert captured side effects); deciding whether a CLI-vs-delegated feature must persist the buffer first. |
| 14 | **Phase 6a outline/symbols — the shared region model, and the "two scanners disagree" trap an adversarial review caught.** (a) **One region scanner, many views.** `core/qmd/model.ts` `scanRegions()` is the single linear pass that classifies every line (YAML front matter `---`…`---`, block HTML comment `<!-- -->`, code fence, ATX heading); `findHeadings`, `findAllCells`, `findCellAtPosition`, and `buildOutline` are thin views over it. **Phase 5's `core/cells.ts` was folded in** (it's now a re-export shim) so cell-finding has ONE implementation. The 17 Phase-5 cell tests are the consolidation regression net — keep them green. (b) **The trap:** Phase 6a first shipped `findHeadings` (front-matter- and fence-aware) and a SEPARATE `findAllCells` (fence-aware only). The two **disagreed on skip-regions** — `findAllCells` happily found a phantom cell inside YAML front matter / an HTML comment / a 4-space-indented fence (CommonMark §4.5 indented code), corrupting both the outline AND Phase 5 run-cell (which shares `findAllCells`). Happy-path tests (97 unit / 25 integration, all green) missed all of it; a 5-lens adversarial review with refute-by-default verification found 8 confirmed, fixed 6 by **unifying into `scanRegions`** (front matter + comments + a 0–3-space fence-indent cap matching the ATX rule), plus stripping the Pandoc `{#sec-id .class}` heading-attribute block from the display name (ubiquitous Quarto construct; the `#sec-` id will drive Phase 6b cross-refs — store it structurally then). (c) **Faithful, env-independent provider test:** `DocumentSymbolProvider` is verified via `vscode.executeDocumentSymbolProvider` in the real test-electron host — no Quarto CLI / Jupyter needed (strongest verification here; extends Learnings #3/#9). Registering a provider needs **no `package.json` contribution** and isn't gated on a context key, so the Learning #13a dead-on-arrival activation trap does not recur. (d) **Deferred (documented scope, not a bug):** setext headings (`===`/`---` underlines) — the model is ATX-only; setext needs `---` disambiguation vs thematic break / front matter and deserves its own TDD pass (backlog). | Any feature consuming the `.qmd` structure (6b cross-refs, 6c citations): consume `scanRegions`/`buildOutline`, don't write a third scanner. When you add a parser that overlaps an existing one, assert they AGREE on skip-regions (front matter, comments, fences) or you'll ship a phantom. Verify any provider via `vscode.execute*Provider` in the host. Lead any model change with a failing unit test (strict TDD). |
| 15 | **Phase 6b cross-references — three label sources over one scanner, two completion-provider traps, and the jupyter-engine render trap.** (a) **One scanner, three sources.** `core/refs.ts` `indexLabels` builds the label index entirely from `findHeadings` (heading `{#sec-…}` ids — `Heading.id`, previously parsed-and-discarded, now kept), `findAllCells` (`#|`/`//|` `label:` cell options), and `findBodyLines` (inline `{#fig-/tbl-/eq-/lst-…}` on prose/heading lines) — all views over `scanRegions` (Learning #14). It writes NO line logic of its own. The Learning-#14 **agreement test** (label-like text in front matter / comments / fences must NOT be indexed) is the guard, and it immediately caught a real **single-line `<!-- … -->` comment leak** (only block comments were skipped before) — fix it in the shared scanner, not in refs. (b) **Two provider traps a happy-path suite misses (caught by adversarial review):** the cross-ref **completion + definition providers fire EVERYWHERE in the `.qmd`** (selector `{language:"quarto"}`; embedded TextMate scopes don't reroute providers) — so `@` in a `{python}`/`{julia}` cell pops the list (decorator/macro) and go-to-def resolves a `@fig-` in cell string literals. **Gate both on a prose predicate** (`isReferenceableLine` = `findBodyLines` membership; includes headings, excludes cells/front-matter/comments). And a single completion `range` from `@`→cursor **duplicates the suffix** when accepting mid-token — use an `{inserting, replacing}` range where `replacing` reaches the token END (forward-scan past the cursor). (c) **The jupyter-engine render trap (extends Learnings #4/#7/#9):** a **python-only** `.qmd` with per-cell `#| eval: false` STILL fails `quarto render` in this shell (no `nbformat`) — the **jupyter engine starts the kernel regardless of per-cell `eval:false`**. `sample.qmd` only renders clean because its `{r}` cell selects the **knitr** engine. For a render-clean python-only fixture, set doc-level **`execute:\n  enabled: false`** in the front matter. (d) **Deferred (documented, not a bug in handled input):** inline `{#fig-…}` inside a CommonMark §4.4 **indented (4-space) code block** is a phantom — a faithful fix must not false-skip 4-space list-item continuation content (model tracks no list context), so it needs its own list-aware TDD pass (backlog). | Phase 6c citations (reuse `crossrefCompletionContext` + `isReferenceableLine`; a bare `@key` is detected/gated the same way) and any provider work: gate completion/definition to the right regions (a whole-doc language selector fires inside cells), and build replace ranges that cover the whole token. Any `.qmd` structure consumer: consume the shared scanner; assert agreement on skip-regions. Any `{python}`-cell test fixture: make it render-clean with doc-level `execute: enabled: false`. |
| 16 | **Phase 6c citations — the front-matter reader, the "don't reuse a token-scanner across token grammars" trap, and parser/adapter robustness.** (a) **The region model skips front matter, so reading `bibliography:` needs its own reader** — `core/frontmatter.ts` `bibliographyPaths` is a focused, no-YAML-lib reader for the one key, handling scalar / flow-list / block-list forms. A minimal hand reader is right for v1, BUT the adversarial review found 4 real YAML-edge defects it first missed: a **zero-indent block list** (`bibliography:` then `- a.bib` flush-left — valid YAML) parsed to `[]`; a **trailing `# comment`** was kept as part of the path (and defeated flow-list detection); an empty quoted scalar returned `['']`. Real front matter is messier than the happy path — test comments, CRLF, indentation variants. (b) **THE BIG TRAP — do not reuse a token-scanner built for a different token grammar.** 6c first reused `crossrefCompletionContext`/`ID_CHAR` (`[A-Za-z0-9_-]`) for citekeys, but **citekeys routinely contain `:`/`.`** (biblatex `Knuth:1984`, DBLP `DBLP:journals/...`, dotted `einstein.1905`). Result: completion **stopped firing after a `:`** and **duplicated the suffix on a mid-token accept** (`@Knuth:1984` → `@Knuth:1984:1984`) — the EXACT finding-E class Learning #15(b) claimed eliminated, silently reintroduced by reuse. Fix: a citation-specific `citationCompletionContext` with a citekey char class (`[A-Za-z0-9_:.+/-]`, trailing-punct-trimmed). When you reuse a scanner/regex for a new token type, re-verify its character class matches the new grammar. (c) **Parser robustness the happy path misses (all 3/3-confirmed):** brace-matching must be **quote-aware** (a stray `{` inside a quoted BibTeX value else makes `matchBrace` consume/discard the rest of the file); **strip a leading UTF-8 BOM before `JSON.parse`** (it throws on a BOM → a BOM-saved CSL-JSON silently loads zero citations; BibTeX via `indexOf("@")` is BOM-immune, so the bug is CSL-only); accept `(`/`)`-delimited entries; type-guard a CSL `date-parts` leaf (`[[null]]` → `year:"null"`). (d) **Faithful tests for layered-defense adapter branches (gate d):** the "missing bib / no bibliography / non-file scheme" safety paths are layered, so no single behavior test isolates one guard — establish discrimination by **temporarily breaking each guard, observing the targeted test go RED, then reverting** (done this session: the early-return break reds no-bib+untitled; a spurious-result break reds missing-bib). A green degradation test isn't faithful until you've seen it fail for the right reason. A fixture whose purpose is a missing bib **cannot be render-clean** (Quarto rejects it) — document that like `render-error.qmd`. | Any feature reading an external file named in front matter (reuse `bibliographyPaths`; resolve relative to `dirname(doc)`); **any reuse of an existing completion/token scanner for a different token type — check the char class first**; any new file-format parser (quote-aware brace matching, BOM strip, never throw on malformed input → `[]`); any adapter degradation path (prove the guard with a break-revert RED, pair positive/negative controls). |
| 17 | **v1 release-prep item 1 — wiring the GitHub remote (verified live, Session 10).** (a) **The repo `rmsharp/vscode_quarto_ext` pre-existed with GitHub auto-init** (a throwaway `LICENSE` + 1-line `README.md`) on an **UNRELATED history**, and its **default branch is `master`, not `main`** (operator's choice). Local `main` was renamed to `master` (`git branch -m`) and reconciled with **`git push -u origin master --force-with-lease`** — discarding the auto-init (we already have a real `LICENSE` + `README.md`). For any future remote wiring: **inspect the remote first** (`git ls-remote origin`, `git show --stat origin/<branch>`, `git merge-base` to detect unrelated histories); expect auto-init; reconcile by force-with-lease, never a junk `--allow-unrelated-histories` merge. (b) **vsce normalizes the repo's `LICENSE` (no extension) to `LICENSE.txt` INSIDE the `.vsix`**, but the working-tree file is `LICENSE` — so a README relative link must target **`LICENSE`** (not `LICENSE.txt`). The marketplace rewrites relative links to absolute GitHub URLs using the `repository` field, which is exactly why Learning #5's relative-link restriction only lifts once `repository` exists. (c) **Dropping `--allow-missing-repository` works the moment a `repository` field is in `package.json`** — vsce reads `package.json`, NOT the git remote, so packaging needs no push. Verified: clean **9-file** `.vsix` (19 KB) without the flag, 190/190 unit green. | The rest of v1 release prep — **item 2** (marketplace metadata: real `publisher`/`icon`/`keywords`/`bugs`/`homepage`, polished `displayName`/`description`, README rewrite) and **item 3** (F5 visual pass + screenshots) — and any future GitHub-remote wiring or marketplace publish. The remote is now wired (`origin` → `master`); `repository` is set; the `package` script is flag-free. |

Art is **original** (a document card + `</>` + "MIT" badge), not Quarto's trademarked logo — the clean-room/licensing posture (Learning #1) extends to branding. `icon` must be ≥128×128; 256×256 used. Relative links (`LICENSE`, `NOTICE`, the `#license--attribution` anchor — note GitHub's double-hyphen slug for "License & attribution") resolve and are marketplace-rewritten via `repository` (Learnings #5/#17). `preview: true` set as the honest 0.0.1 first-listing state. | 49 | **A per-claim adversarial verify pass with tool access (not just a synthesis agent) is where competitive-research defects actually surface — 45% of rows had one (Session 42, Posit feature-comparison doc).** Built `docs/POSIT-COMPARISON.md` (31 feature-parity rows vs. Posit's official AGPL-3.0 Quarto extension) via a `Workflow`: 5 parallel web-research agents by domain → 1 synthesis agent merging into a draft matrix → 31 independent verify agents, one per row, each re-grepping OUR repo and re-fetching every cited Posit URL, explicitly instructed to find problems rather than confirm. **14 of 31 rows (45%) had a real, confirmed defect at first draft** — none on our own side (every `ourStatus`/`ourEvidence` claim, grounded from `ROADMAP.md`+code before research began, survived verification untouched); all 14 were either (a) stale Posit-side citations presented as current (a 2022 changelog entry for a feature since redesigned — verified by pulling the LIVE `package.json`/source at today's commit, not just the changelog), (b) a citation that didn't support its own quote (fetched twice independently and the exact quoted string wasn't on the page — likely synthesized/misremembered by the research agent, not maliciously fabricated), (c) a citation pointing at the wrong URL for an otherwise-true fact (the right fact existed, just at a different page than named), (d) an overclaim about OUR OWN code (calling a deliberately-capped 1-level-deep completion "recursive"/"3+", contradicted by our own function's docstring), (e) an undercounted gap (claimed we're missing 2 commands, verified 4), or (f) a direction-reversal (claimed a Posit advantage that, on re-verification against their CURRENT source, turned out to be something Posit removed years ago and never restored — we were actually ahead). **🔑 The failure mode this catches is specific to competitive/multi-source research: a synthesis agent under time/token pressure tends to accept its own research agents' claims at face value and doesn't re-fetch to confirm a citation still says what it's quoted as saying "as of today," nor re-check whether a claim about OUR OWN codebase (which the synthesis agent did NOT independently verify, only merged) is precisely worded.** The fix is structural, not "be more careful": give a dedicated verify-stage agent BOTH read access to our repo (Bash/Grep) AND live web access (WebFetch) to independently re-derive each claim from primary sources, one claim per agent so an agent's attention isn't split across 31 claims. Regular, not campaign-scale research (a 31-row doc, ~22 min wall-clock, ~1.47M subagent tokens) still benefited enormously from this — it is not only for exhaustive/high-stakes verification campaigns. | Any deliverable that makes multiple comparative or externally-sourced factual claims (competitive analysis, "how does X do it" research, any doc citing a third party's current behavior): budget a dedicated adversarial-verify stage — one agent per discrete claim, with tool access to re-derive both sides independently — as a separate pipeline stage after synthesis, not folded into the synthesis agent's own pass. Fixing the general policy (not a `name === "copyright"` special case) was proportional BECAUSE the inventory confirmed no other collision would regress — skipping that inventory would have made "generic vs. special-cased" a guess instead of a verified call. (b) **DEVELOPMENT_WORKSTREAM.md's explicit "not for one-off fixes... if it's a single bug with a clear fix, just fix it" carve-out applied correctly here** — no campaign tracker, no multi-session decomposition; strict TDD (RED via a fixture mirroring the real collision — the poorer entry inserted FIRST, matching the real schema's actual JSON key order, since `Map`/`Object.entries` iteration order is insertion order for string keys — then the minimal `Map`-based richest-wins fix) plus the project's standing gate-d break-revert convention (forcing `quartoSharePath` to throw) were still the right bar for a pure bugfix session, not just for feature slices. (c) **A `Map<name, SchemaField>` (not an array + `Set<string>`) makes "keep the richer of two collisions, preserve first-seen ORDER" trivial**: `.set()` on an existing key replaces its VALUE without moving its position in iteration order, so richness-comparison and position-stability are independent concerns — no separate index-tracking needed. 483 unit (+1) / 172 integration (+1); clean 35-file `.vsix`; compile clean. | Any shared dedup/merge function found buggy for one named instance: grep the real data for every OTHER instance of the same collision shape before deciding whether the fix should be generic or name-specific — a generic policy is safe to ship once you've confirmed no other instance's behavior regresses (a tie is not a regression). A single, clearly-scoped bug (not a repeating pattern needing campaign tracking) still gets the full strict-TDD + gate-d break-revert bar — DEVELOPMENT_WORKSTREAM.md's "campaigns only" framing narrows the PROCESS overhead (no tracker table, no multi-session plan), not the VERIFICATION bar. | 46 | **CLAUDE.md size-management — extract a runaway append-only section into its own committed, non-auto-loaded file (Session 39).** `CLAUDE.md`'s "Project-specific Learnings" table had grown to 45 rows / 159 KB of the file's 164 KB (~97%) over 38 sessions — and `CLAUDE.md` is injected in full into every session's context (confirmed via the system-reminder at session start), so every session was paying that cost regardless of relevance. Extracted the table verbatim into a new `PROJECT_LEARNINGS.md` at the project root, leaving a short pointer paragraph in `CLAUDE.md`'s "Project-specific Learnings" subsection (net: CLAUDE.md 164 KB → 5.8 KB). (a) **🔑 The pointer MUST be a plain Markdown link (`[text](PROJECT_LEARNINGS.md)`), never an `@`-import (`@PROJECT_LEARNINGS.md`) — an `@`-import auto-expands into every session's context exactly like the inline table did, defeating the entire point of the extraction** (operator-flagged mid-task before the edit was made — the harness treats `@path` specially even inside prose). Grep any future extraction's pointer text for a stray leading `@` before committing. (b) **Move large content with tooling, never by retyping.** Used `sed -n` to locate exact line boundaries, a Python script to slice-and-replace `CLAUDE.md` in place, and — the load-bearing verification step — `diff <(sed -n '<old-range>p' CLAUDE.md-before) <(sed -n '<new-range>p' PROJECT_LEARNINGS.md)` to prove the moved content is BYTE-IDENTICAL before deleting it from the source. A 160 KB block is not something to hand-copy into an `Edit` `old_string`/`new_string` pair — the tool call itself becomes the risk. (c) **Check whether the extracted heading is a hard-coded anchor in files you cannot edit before assuming a rename or restructure is free.** `SESSION_RUNNER.md` (synced, byte-identical, canonical-only) instructs sessions to "put project learnings in your CLAUDE.md → Project-Specific Methodology Adaptations → Project-specific Learnings subsection" — grepped `SESSION_RUNNER.md`/`BOOTSTRAP.md`/`CLAUDE_TEMPLATE.md`/`docs/methodology/HOW_TO_USE.md` for that exact heading string first; all four are synced/canonical and unelidable. The fix was to KEEP the heading text identical and only change what's under it to a pointer — satisfying the synced instruction's letter (the heading still exists, still in CLAUDE.md) while relocating the payload. Renaming or removing the heading itself would have silently broken every synced file's instruction with no way to fix the synced side. (d) **A pure-content-move needs no unit test (CLAUDE.md's own TDD-mandate exemption clause: "pure declarative/config/doc edits with no logic") but still needs the two normal checks** — `npm run compile` (clean; zero `src/**` touched) and `python3 methodology_dashboard.py` (unchanged 78/100, same pre-existing CRITICAL flag) — plus a repo-wide grep for the old heading text and for any stray `@`-import syntax, since a docs-restructure's failure mode is a dangling reference outside the diff's obvious blast radius (Learning #7/#10 applied to a file split rather than a citation). | Any future CLAUDE.md (or other always-loaded context file) subsection that has grown large and append-only (this table, a decision log, a fixture inventory): extract to a project-owned, git-committed sibling file; point to it with a **plain Markdown link, never an `@`-import**; move content via `sed`/scripted slicing + a byte-exact `diff`, never by retyping; grep every synced/canonical file for a hard-coded reference to the heading you're touching BEFORE renaming or removing it — keep the heading stable and relocate only the payload if any synced file depends on it; verify with the project's normal doc-only checks (compile + dashboard) plus a repo-wide grep for the old content and for accidental auto-import syntax. |

Independently re-run the single most load-bearing empirical test with a second agent before locking a design decision on it, exactly as you would adversarially verify a factual claim in a research doc. |

| 73 | **Quarto's own `.qmd` reader (Pandoc's `markdown` format, NOT `gfm`/`commonmark`) resolves the setext-heading "`---` disambiguation dragon" the backlog item itself flagged as the hard part — but not the way CommonMark's spec describes it, and empirical grounding against the real CLI (both Quarto's bundled Pandoc and a separate system `pandoc` binary, cross-checked) surfaced 3 genuinely surprising rules no amount of spec-reading would have found (Session 66, implementing setext heading support in the outline, `BACKLOG.md` Polish/deferred item).** (a) **A 2+-line paragraph does NOT promote to a setext heading in Pandoc's `markdown` reader** — unlike `gfm`/`commonmark` (verified: identical input promotes under `-f gfm`/`-f commonmark` but stays a plain paragraph, underline included as literal trailing text, under `-f markdown`). This dissolved what looked like the biggest scoping decision (multi-line heading text) into a non-issue: single-line-only isn't a pragmatic simplification, it's the CORRECT, faithful behavior for `.qmd`'s actual reader. (b) **A setext underline immediately following an ATX heading line (no blank line) swallows the ATX line's literal text — INCLUDING its `#` markers — into the setext heading**, e.g. `"# ATX Heading\n---"` renders `<h2># ATX Heading</h2>`, not two separate blocks. This is REAL Pandoc behavior (reproduced with plain `pandoc -f markdown`, not a Quarto-specific artifact) but was deliberately NOT replicated: a pre-existing, currently-passing unit test (`qmd-model.test.ts`, "does not treat a `---` that is not at line 0 as front matter") already asserts the OPPOSITE (both stay separate ATX headings) for an unrelated reason, so replicating Pandoc's quirk here would have required breaking or rewriting established, unrelated test coverage for an extremely rare adjacency — the divergence is disclosed in both the model's docstring and a dedicated regression test, not silently absorbed. (c) **A lone bullet-list item (`-`/`*`/`+` marker) immediately followed by an underline gets NESTED inside the list** (`<li><h2>text</h2></li>`, marker stripped) — but an ORDERED-list marker (`1.`) or a block-quote marker (`>`) does NOT nest; both stay literal heading text with the marker included verbatim. A flat, list-unaware regex scanner (this model tracks no list/blockquote context, matching the pre-existing accepted CommonMark-indented-code-block gap) would silently produce a heading with a WRONG name (the literal `"- solo item"`, marker included) for the bullet-list case if left unguarded — caught via reasoning, then confirmed empirically, and fixed with a narrow guard (`BULLET_LIST_MARKER`) that declines (false negative) rather than mis-titles; the ordered-list/blockquote cases needed NO guard since the general mechanism already reproduces their literal-inclusion behavior correctly. All three findings came from directly testing edge-case fixtures against the real CLI before writing any implementation code (`ARCHITECTURE`/`DEVELOPMENT_WORKSTREAM`'s "grounding, not documentation-level verification" discipline, Learnings #6/#52/#62 lineage) — none are documented in CommonMark's own spec, since Pandoc's `markdown` reader is a DIFFERENT, older dialect with its own extension-gated behavior. | Before implementing ANY Markdown/CommonMark-adjacent parsing logic for a `.qmd` file, verify against Pandoc's actual `markdown` reader specifically (`pandoc -f markdown`, or `quarto render`/`quarto pandoc`) — NOT against the CommonMark spec, NOT against `gfm`, and not from general Markdown knowledge. The three readers genuinely disagree on block-level disambiguation rules (multi-line setext promotion, block-adjacency swallowing, list-nesting-vs-literal-inclusion), and `.qmd` always uses Pandoc's own `markdown` format. When a flat, context-unaware regex scanner (this model's whole architecture) would need to fabricate structural nesting to match a reader's real behavior (e.g. Pandoc's list-item swallowing), prefer declining/false-negative over emitting a structurally-wrong result with fabricated text — and write a same-file regression test locking in the deliberate divergence, not just a comment. |

| 75 | **VS Code's pull-based request-forwarding architecture (`vscode.executeCompletionItemProvider` etc. — this project's whole `src/providers/embedded.ts` design) has a hard, documented ceiling: it cannot serve diagnostics, and the reason is not a missing feature to work around but a fundamentally different delivery model (Session 68, planning `BACKLOG.md` item 10, code-cell diagnostics forwarding).** Diagnostics are push-based (a language server proactively publishes via a `DiagnosticCollection`, on its own schedule) — VS Code's own Extension API docs state directly that request forwarding "does not work with diagnostics errors... does not support diagnostic providers that can 'pull.'" When a competitor's own public PR/changelog prose describes an unexpectedly heavy architecture for something that sounds like it should be simple, take that as a signal to verify firsthand (a scratch, throwaway Extension Development Host test — write, run, observe, delete, never commit) before assuming a lighter approach will work; three convergent independent sources (official docs, your own empirical test, a competitor's own admission) is enough to change a plan's recommended architecture, not just enough to flag a risk. |

| 77 | **When forwarding a request to a per-computation virtual document via `vscode.executeXxxProvider`, not every provider family tolerates a REUSED vdoc URI the same way — test each one's caching behavior independently rather than assuming the existing recipe generalizes (Session 70, planning `BACKLOG.md` item 11, outline granularity / in-cell code symbols).** This project's existing `src/providers/embedded.ts` forwards completion/hover/definition/signature-help against a STABLE per-(document, language) vdoc URI, rebuilt-per-request (`VirtualDocStore`) — and a firsthand empirical test this session confirmed `vscode.executeCompletionItemProvider` correctly reflects an edit on that reused URI (no staleness). A 21-agent adversarial review (5 finder lenses × 2-skeptic refutation) surfaced SIX real survivors that green tests missed: the HIGH session-identity race, a HIGH "restart branch untested" coverage gap, the MEDIUM flow-collection garbage-token bug (`format: {html: default}` — a valid YAML flow mapping — parsed as one opaque `--to {html: default}` token instead of `["html"]`, because the scalar branch fired before the block branch and `unquote` doesn't strip `{`/`[`), a MEDIUM untested `["html"]` fallback (a `:[]` mutation → silent no-op survived green), a MEDIUM weak gate-d discriminator (the sole fixture declared exactly `["html","docx"]`, byte-identical to a plausible hardcode, so a `parseDeclaredFormats(...)`→`["html","docx"]` literal severing the parser from the picker survived), and a LOW `starting`-guard-drops-differing-format-during-startup race. So the guard is a correct-by-construction defensive fix, not a break-revert-proven one; what IS break-revert-proven is finding #3's deterministic coverage (deleting the restart-branch dispose → the "html server must be reaped" assertion goes red) and finding #4/#5's fallback (removing `["html"]` → the no-format test goes red). Distinguishing "correct by construction, race not reproducible here" from "break-revert-proven" in the write-up is the honest close-out, not claiming a red that never happened. Separately, item 15's own "moderate scope" BACKLOG framing understated `previewScript` (Posit's `quartoRenderScriptActive` context key needs content-scanning a `.py`/`.jl`/`.r` script for `# %%` percent-cells — no precedent in this codebase, where the only context key `quarto.inCodeCell` is cursor-driven); surfaced to the operator via `AskUserQuestion` (the item-14/Learning #87 pattern) → scoped this session to `previewFormat` only, `previewScript` deferred to its own session. Grounded the CLI mechanics firsthand and safely: `quarto preview <file> --no-browser --to <fmt>` verified by running it with `--timeout <n>` so the server SELF-EXITS (no orphan, no manual kill needed) — the way to empirically test a long-lived-server CLI command without leaving a process behind. | When extending a manager that owns per-key lifecycle state (one live process/panel/connection per document/uri) with a new operation that can REPLACE the entry for a key mid-lifetime (restart, re-open, switch-variant), audit EVERY late-firing handler (`close`/`exit`/`error`/timeout/`onDidDispose`) that was written keyed on that key alone: capture the specific `session`/`instance` object in the handler's closure and guard side effects on `map.get(key) === thatObject`, because "the entry still exists at this key" no longer implies "it is the same entry this handler belongs to." Run the standing adversarial-review `Workflow` on the shipped slice even when every layer is green — a "restart/replace" branch that works in the happy path but is never re-invoked by a from-zero test is exactly the marquee behavior the review catches (here 6 real survivors from an all-green slice). To test a CLI that spawns a long-lived server, use its own self-exit/timeout flag (`quarto preview … --timeout N`) rather than spawning-and-killing. And in close-out, distinguish a correct-by-construction fix for a non-deterministically-reproducible race from a break-revert-proven one — write which is which, never imply a red you did not observe. |

| 92 | **A regex copied verbatim from a CLI can be a performance bug in an editor even when it is functionally correct — and an all-accept test battery cannot tell you the content half of a predicate is dead.** Two independent defects in one small pure detector, both invisible to a green suite. (1) **ReDoS by inheritance.** `src/core/render-script.ts`'s spin regex was copied from Quarto's `isKnitrSpinScript` (quarto.js:28695), including a redundant `\s*` between the lazy `[\s\S]+?` and `#'`. Redundant ≠ harmless: it is *ambiguous* with the lazy quantifier, so a FAILING match (a `#' ---` header opened and never closed — exactly what a user mid-edit has) backtracks **quadratically** in the longest contiguous whitespace run. 80k blank lines = **3.7 seconds** with the extension host blocked. Quarto gets away with it because the CLI runs it once per render in a Deno subprocess; VS Code runs it on a single shared UI thread. Deleting one `\s*` → 0.03 ms, provably same language. **The lesson is not "don't copy the CLI" — it is that a predicate's *cost model* does not transfer across execution contexts even when its *semantics* do.** The plan had even certified this regex as "cheap on every keystroke" *because* it was lazy — exactly backwards, and the next slice was designed to rely on that certification. (2) **The surviving mutant.** Every `.r`/`.R` case in the 12-test battery was an ACCEPT, so `SPIN_HEADER.test(text)` was asserted by nothing: mutating the impl to `return ext === SPIN_EXTENSION` ("every `.r` file is a render script") passed all 738 tests. A battery built by walking a plan's table of *positive* examples reproduces the plan's blind spots. For any `A && B` predicate, ask which test would fail if `B` were deleted — if none, `B` is untested no matter how many tests pass. | When copying a regex or algorithm from a CLI/batch tool into an editor extension (or any latency-sensitive, single-threaded host): re-derive its worst-case cost in the NEW context — an unclosed-delimiter/failing-match input is the one to time, not the happy path — and add a timing lock. When writing a test battery for a boolean predicate: for each conjunct, write the test that dies if that conjunct is deleted, and break-revert-prove it against that exact mutant. Both defects here were found by the standing adversarial-review `Workflow` on an all-green slice, not by the tests. |

| 94 | **A test double registered on the same axis the real dependency discriminates by cannot detect that the real dependency REJECTS that axis — and a 100%-green suite will hide a totally dead feature (Session 86, PLANNING item 16; discovered a SHIPPED defect, now BACKLOG item 18).** This project's embedded-language forwarding (Phase 6e completion/hover/go-to-def/signature-help, plus in-cell outline symbols and format-cell) routes requests through a **virtual document under a CUSTOM URI scheme** (`quarto-embedded`, `quarto-outline-symbols`, `quarto-format-cell`). Real language servers filter by **scheme** in their LSP `documentSelector` (typically `file:`/`untitled:`/`vscode-notebook-cell:`), so **no provider is ever registered for our vdoc**: `executeXxxProvider` returns nothing, with **no error and no warning**. The feature has been **dead in production for `{python}` since it shipped**, while every one of its tests passed. The reason is mechanical, not sloppiness: each stand-in is registered as **`{ scheme: <our-custom-scheme> }`** — a selector pinned to *precisely the axis* the real server discriminates on. Such a double asserts "a request routed through our scheme reaches a provider registered on our scheme," which is trivially true and says **nothing** about whether any *real* server registers there. Adding more stand-in tests can never detect this; only a test against the **real dependency** can, and it needs a **control** proving the real dependency was alive (otherwise "no results" is indistinguishable from "the server never started"). Generalization: whenever a double stands in for an external dependency, ask *what does the real thing discriminate on?* (scheme, content-type, auth scope, protocol version, file extension) — and make sure the double is **not** keyed on that same thing. If it is, the test is a tautology wearing a green checkmark. | Session 86 (planning item 16) — the spike that refuted item 16's premise and uncovered the shipped defect; `docs/planning/2026-07-12-embedded-lsp-scheme-and-semantic-tokens-plan.md` §3/§10.1 | When writing ANY test double for an external dependency (a language server, an API client, a CLI, a plugin host). Identify the axis the real dependency filters/dispatches on, and ensure the double does not key on that same axis. | 99 | **When you layer a semantic feature over an existing one, the incumbent is EVIDENCE — read what it already gets right before "improving" it.** Session 90's D4 decision looked like arithmetic: our legend dropped 36% of real Pylance's tokens, so carry the foreign names and recover them. So the set of names with **no** scope entry is exactly the set safe to carry bare — the same judgement the author already made, read back out of their manifest. | 101 | **A per-key guard cannot cover a global-teardown race — the teardown has no key to invalidate, and the racing operation may not be registered under any key yet.** Session 88 fixed the document-close vdoc-strand race with a PER-DOCUMENT epoch: `disposeVdocs(docUri)` is handed the exact key that closed and bumps *that* epoch, so an in-flight `ensureVdoc` snapshotting `epochOf(key.docUri)` before its awaits sees it move. The correct primitive for a GLOBAL teardown is a single monotonic **global** generation, snapshotted before the awaits and re-checked after: it invalidates every in-flight operation at once, keyed or not. The corollary that made it robust: put the bump **synchronous and FIRST**, before any await, because the teardown is itself fire-and-forget — `deactivate()` runs `void disposeAllVdocs()` and never awaits it, so the guard's correctness must not depend on the teardown's own async work completing. Two independent signals said "trivial" (a one-line filed fix; a green build), and both were wrong about the shape; only writing the failing test first surfaced it. | Session 91 (the `disposeAllVdocs` deactivate-strand fix; the filed "one line, per-owner" framing refuted by the RED test, then confirmed correct by a 9-agent review with 5/6 lenses empty) | Any time you extend a per-entity concurrency guard (per-document, per-request, per-connection epoch) to a whole-system teardown (deactivate, shutdown, dispose-all). Ask: what key does the teardown bump, and is the racing operation guaranteed to be under that key by the time it resumes? If either answer is "none"/"no", reach for a single monotonic global generation, bumped synchronously before any await — not a per-key one. | 110 | **The KIND of provider a test double registers is a branch-selecting axis — a stand-in of the wrong kind silently relocates the code under test onto a path production never takes, and the suite stays green while the real branch is never exercised.** Learning #94 found this on the *scheme* axis (every stand-in registered on our custom URI scheme — the exact axis real servers discriminate by — so a 100%-green suite hid a totally dead feature). And before recording any race/interleaving claim: name the AWAIT that opens the window, then prove it with a probe carrying a POSITIVE CONTROL — and never promote a prose sentence in your own repo to "measured". |

| 111 | **A filed fix is a hypothesis, not a design — run it before you believe it, and re-derive the mechanism from the event loop rather than from the item's own vocabulary.** `BACKLOG:102` filed both a mechanism ("when an untitled-doc forward **wins** the deactivate **race**") and a fix ("move the resets OUT of the `if`, and have `disposeAllVdocs` observe `fallbackDirPromise` … so a raced deactivate still `rmdir`s"). Reading "race" as "occasional" also mis-sizes severity in the *safe* direction, which is the kind of error that survives review. (2) **The filed fix was insufficient, and only running it revealed why:** the directory still survived, EMPTY (`survived=true contents=[]`) — the in-flight forward writes its file before the non-recursive `rmdir` lands, `rmdir` fails ENOTEMPTY, and the forward's own epoch guard then deletes the file, leaving precisely the empty directory the fix existed to reclaim. The real fix needed a third change the item never contemplated (bail *before* writing a file you are about to delete). Corollary, learned the same session: when the observation contradicts your model, say so in the comment. The first draft of that guard explained itself with an unverified promise-resume-order theory ("this forward attached first, so it always resumes first"); a probe contradicted it, so the shipped comment states what was *measured* (cleanup is unreliable without the guard, reliable with it) and explicitly marks the interleaving as uncharacterized. **When to apply:** any session implementing a fix a previous session *filed*. Implement it, run it, and treat both its mechanism and its remedy as claims under test — and if it passes for a reason you cannot name, say that in the code rather than inventing one. |

One command refuted it: `/^quarto-mit-vdoc-([0-9]+)-[A-Za-z0-9]{6}$/.exec("quarto-mit-vdoc-548278u7zTF")` → **null**. The real failure mode was the *opposite class*: a silent, total, safe-direction leak (the sweep reclaims nothing, ever), not a wrong-PID delete. Three independent review lenses caught it; the author did not. **The asymmetry that makes this a trap:** you feel *maximally* grounded right after a firsthand grounding pass — which is exactly when a plausible sentence from your own fleet's prose slides in unexamined, because it arrived wearing the same evidence-shaped clothes as the measurements around it. A subagent's *measured output* and its *narrative summary of that output* are different artifacts with different reliability, and the summary is where the errors live. **When to apply:** whenever a claim reaches your artifact from a subagent rather than from your own hands — a probe result, a review finding, a "measured" figure in a fleet report. If a claim carries a label like "Measured", the label is a promise you must be able to re-execute *in the artifact's own terms* — if you cannot re-run it in one command, it is not measured, it is repeated. Corollary, learned the same session: adversarial review is worth running against your **own** draft, not just your predecessor's — and its *refuted* findings can still be the most valuable thing in it (S102's PID-namespace finding was refuted on its "this is routine" premise, yet the guard was adopted anyway once the release status showed the grammar locks at first publish — the refutation improved the reason, not the decision). |

The **leak** I described comes from a hostname *change* (DHCP/rename → tags differ → skip) — a different event entirely, which I conflated with the collision. Both are `npm audit fix --force` artifacts, not the minimal fix. The pin crosses mocha's declared `^6.0.2`, but that is inert here — verified, not assumed: no `.mocharc*`, no `--parallel` in any script, so serialize-javascript (mocha's parallel-reporter-only dep) is never executed; the 333-test integration suite passing unchanged confirms it. So the mocha MAJOR bump the "hygiene" framing tempts you toward is pure added risk for zero audit benefit — keep it pinned. (b) **A dev-dependency audit fix is runtime-verified for free by an integration suite that loads the actual BUNDLE, so it is not FM #24 (build-passes-ship-it).** The two upgrades verify on different surfaces: the unit runner (`vitest run`, 834 tests, count-unchanged = no silent test-drop) exercises the *runner* bump; the integration suite (`@vscode/test-electron`, 333 tests in a real Extension Development Host that loads `dist/extension.js`) exercises the *bundler* bump's output at runtime. (2) A cardinal-sin-risk plan warrants an independent adversarial panel even after thorough author grounding — three sessions running, the panel beat two firsthand passes; state safety invariants as REACHABILITY claims, not universals. |

| 154 | **A regression LOCK only locks if its inputs would make the DEFECT fire — assert BOTH sides of a forked invariant, and choose a value the bug actually mis-handles; a lock that passes equally with OR without the bug locks nothing.** Shipping S141's `execute:`-value slice, the central dragon (S140 #1) was that the value enumerator and the unknown-KEY enumerator SHARE a container predicate, so adding `execute` to the shared `PROJECT_CONFIG_CONTAINERS` would make the KEY feature flag unknown execute keys — a cardinal-sin FP (quarto ACCEPTS `custom-thing: whatever`, exit 0). Two lock-design refinements made the regression tests actually bite: (1) **Assert BOTH sides of the fork.** A test that only asserts `findProjectConfigKeyLines("execute:…") === []` passes even if NEITHER enumerator saw execute — it never proves the predicates DIVERGE. The lock ALSO asserts the VALUE enumerator DOES see execute (`.map(v=>v.container) === ["execute","execute"]`), so it turns red the moment someone re-merges the predicates (widening the KEY set OR narrowing the value set). (2) **Pick a value the bug mis-handles for a collision lock.** The depth-2 name-collision safe-FN (`execute.knitr.cache`, resolved BY PATH → `knitr` ∉ `CURATED_EXECUTE_KEYS` → undefined → skip) must be locked with `knitr.cache: banana` — a value the BUGGY bare-name resolution WOULD flag (`banana` ∉ the closed depth-1 `execute.cache` enum). A depth-1-VALID value (`knitr.cache: true`) passes identically under BOTH correct path-based AND buggy bare-name resolution — locking nothing. (3) A "valid" (zero-OUR-diagnostics) fixture's contract is "zero of OUR diagnostics", NOT "renders clean": a deliberate safe-FN line (`knitr.cache: banana` — quarto exit-1, we silent by design) legitimately lives in the valid fixture, documented; the feature's contract ≠ quarto-cleanliness. The mandatory 4-lens §9 review (`wf_208f743b-ced`, 220+ probes) + a 37-case author FP battery both returned 0 cardinal-sin FPs — the clean-panel-after-front-loaded-catch pattern (the plan front-loaded dragon 1 into the KEY-isolation lock; cf. #152). | When writing a regression LOCK for a forked invariant or a path-vs-bare-name resolution: (a) assert BOTH sides so re-merging the fork turns it red — one-sided assertions pass vacuously; (b) choose lock inputs the DEFECT would actually mis-handle (a value invalid for the colliding sibling), not ones both correct and buggy code accept; (c) a "valid"/zero-diagnostics fixture may hold a documented safe-FN line quarto rejects — its contract is your feature's silence, not quarto-cleanliness. |

| 156 | **When a GO-LIVE edit WIDENS a recognized-set (adds a name to a container/keyword set), the pre-existing tests that used that name as a NEGATIVE ("unknown"/"not recognized") example go RED — and that RED is the go-live SIGNAL, not a regression; reconcile them by swapping the example to a still-negative value, never by deleting the assertion. | 157 | **When you build a validator that MIMICS a tool's behavior, ground its rule against the exact LAYER whose output you reproduce — a tool often has multiple layers that DISAGREE, and modeling on the wrong one ships cardinal-sin false positives that firsthand grounding of the wrong layer will "confirm."** Planning S144's format-NAME validation (flag `format: banana` matching `quarto render`), I extracted quarto's acceptance rule from `parseFormatString`/`breakFormatString` (quarto.js:41317/41365) and built a two-path predicate (base-token + last-hyphen-suffix). Why two firsthand passes missed it: my modifier probe used the `+`-delimited `foo-html+smart` (works under BOTH predicates because `lastIndexOf('-')` still precedes the base), never the `-`-delimited `foo-html-smart`; and I never probed `.lua` at all — I grounded the CASES my (wrong) mental model predicted, not the cases that would DISTINGUISH the layers. | 158 | **When you mirror a validator whose regex is BUILT FROM A STRING (`regexSchema("…")` / `new RegExp("…")`), copy the COMPILED pattern's semantics — not the source string's apparent intent: a `\.` written in the source is NOT a literal dot in the compiled regex, because the STRING escape collapses `\.` to a bare `.` (a wildcard) before RegExp ever sees it.** S144's §9 review had already corrected the format-NAME predicate to mirror the SCHEMA layer `makeFrontMatterFormatSchema` (Learning #157) — an `anyOf` of `^(.+-)?<name>([-+].+)?$` + `^.+\.lua$`. Quarto therefore ACCEPTS any name of ≥2 chars followed by `lua` (`foolua`, `aalua`, `abclua`, `htmlua`), NOT only a literal `.lua`. (Two of the 4 lenses failed on a StructuredOutput retry cap; I discharged fp-cardinal firsthand via that 50-name battery and doc-drift via a whole-corpus grep.) This is the FOURTH consecutive family cluster (cf. #151/#153/#157) where the §9 panel beat thorough firsthand author passes on a cardinal-sin — and the sharpest: it beat #157's OWN correction, which fixed the LAYER but still transcribed that layer's regex-SOURCE dot as a literal. Sibling of #157 (right layer) at one level deeper: right layer, right regex SOURCE-vs-COMPILED semantics. | When mirroring a tool's regex-based validation: (1) if the tool builds its regex from a STRING (`regexSchema`/`new RegExp("…")`), mentally (or actually) run the string through JS string-escape collapse FIRST — `\.`→`.`, `\d` stays, etc. — and mirror the RESULTING compiled pattern, not the source text; a `\.` in a `new RegExp("…")` string is a wildcard, in a `/…/` literal it is a literal dot. | 160 | **A derived bit that LOOSENS a check is not a copy of the sibling bit that TIGHTENS one — the fold operator inverts, and the completeness standard is parity with the GATE that reads the bit, not with the data format.** Shipping the null-arm fix (S147, prerequisite P of the S146 plan), the new `acceptsNull` sat beside three existing annotators (`valuesClosed`, `numericMemberEnum`, `scalarType`) that all prove a RESTRICTION, so the obvious move was to mirror one arm-for-arm. Two things do not carry over. (a) **The `anyOf` fold inverts.** The siblings fold with AND (every arm must be closed / numeric); an ADMISSION folds with OR — one null-admitting arm makes the whole field admit null. Copying the sibling's AND would have left the field flagging a value quarto accepts, i.e. reproduced the exact cardinal-sin FP the slice existed to remove. Same for the risk polarity: over-setting `acceptsNull` is a safe false negative, while a MISSED arm is the false positive — the opposite of `valuesClosed`, where over-setting is the danger. (b) **"Walk every arm" needs a target.** The mandatory §9 review found two null-bearing shapes the walk does NOT handle (a bare `null` `anyOf` member, `epub-subdirectory`; and the `{null:{…}}` type wrapper, `out-width`) and correctly returned CLEAN anyway — because the bit is only ever READ behind the `valuesClosed` gate, and `closednessOfSchema` returns OPEN for both shapes, so the matcher returns before consulting it. The right completeness standard was therefore parity with the **gate's own walk**, not with the DSL's whole null vocabulary. I verified that firsthand rather than accepting it, including the adversarial variants where such an arm sits beside only-closed arms (the sole way the claim could fail), and recorded the reasoning in the function's doc comment so the next reviewer does not re-litigate it. **Corollary that cost a real count:** an indirection arm you do not traverse silently turns an "exhaustive" scan into a lower bound. S146's `nullscan.ts` reported "exactly 3 fields in all of Quarto 1.7.33" because its walk tested `node.ref` as an object when the DSL makes it a **string** — so it never resolved into `definitions.yml` and missed a 4th null-admitting name (`output-file`). The miss was invisible precisely because the 4th resolves OPEN and so was never a false positive; nothing downstream disagreed. | When adding a derived annotation bit to a family of existing ones: first ask whether it RESTRICTS or ADMITS, and re-derive every fold operator and the risk polarity from that answer instead of copying a sibling. Then set the completeness target from the gate that READS the bit, not from the raw schema. And whenever a scan's output is a COUNT used as a blast radius, prove its arm coverage against the consumer's own walk — especially every indirection arm (`ref`/`$ref`/include), whose type in the DSL (string vs object) is exactly what a hand-written walk gets wrong. |

| 162 | **A fix that works by ROUTING something through a shared path only holds for inputs that REACH that path — so when you write the premise into a comment ("X is now handled by the same tail as everything else"), the very next move is to enumerate the early exits ahead of it and construct the input that takes one.** Shipping the column-0 document-key slice (S149, ③ of the S146 plan), the whole design was "route column-0 scalars through the SHARED emission tail, which also arms the multi-line continuation guard for them" — and that is genuinely what fixed the three measured Defect-B false positives. | 163 | **A ledger that is complete is not the same as a file that is clean — and the cleanup is where the losses hide.** `BACKLOG.md` had accumulated **115 KB of completed work (46% of the file, 35 top-level `[x]` blocks + 41 nested)** across ~150 sessions, despite its own header rule and SESSION_RUNNER Phase 3F both saying completed items are removed in the commit that records them. Measured: that document renders exit 1, and removing the `{r}` cell renders exit 0. **When to apply:** any time a fix replaces a constant with a lookup table sourced from another tool — verify the EFFECTIVE table (grep for runtime overlays, not just the literal), and ask separately whether each new row is REACHABLE and VALIDATED by that tool. Any time a detector is widened — grep every consumer for re-derivation from raw input. Any time a control is added to a shared fixture — re-measure the fixture, because a control is part of the input. | S161 §9 review (`wf_c7cd5eb0-9af`, 6 lenses, 34 agents, `agents_error:0`, ~1.99M subagent tokens; 5 findings, all confirmed firsthand by the session before acting — 2 were defects in its own work and fixed, 3 were pre-existing with distinct root causes and filed). The engine-scope and closer-in-span FPs were caught by the session's own layered verification before the review ran. | When swapping a hard-coded constant for another tool's table: confirm the effective table (runtime overlays), and check reachability + validation per row, not just the value. When widening any detector: re-audit consumers that re-derive spans/keys from raw text, and ship a BOUND rather than duplicating the grammar. When adding a non-vacuity control to a test fixture: re-measure the fixture against ground truth, since the control is itself input. |
| 175 | **A universal-negative justification ("this costs no true positive", "this key is unvalidated") needs an EXHAUSTIVE sweep over the domain it quantifies — a handful of probes will confirm it and still be wrong, especially along a variable you already know changes the verdict.** S162 suppressed cell-option validation in quarto's two cell-HANDLER languages and justified it with "the suppression costs no true positive", generalised from five keys measured in a markdown-engine document. The §9 review disputed it; an exhaustive sweep of all 47 keys the feature can flag, one render each, in BOTH engines, showed 46/47 exit 0 under markdown (the one exception being a field we could never flag anyway) but exactly one real value-dependent failure under knitr (`include`) — a true positive the fix gave up. The same error shape appeared twice more in the same session: `theme: banana` renders exit 0, so the docstring called `theme` unenforced, but the schema is `null|string` and `theme: [1,2]`/`42` render exit 1; and `{mermaid}` + `#| echo: banana` renders exit 0 only because the fixture had no `{r}` cell — S161's OWN Learning #174c had already recorded that an `{r}` cell makes the document knitr. Each time the discriminating variable was one the session already knew about and had not varied. A companion failure, same root: the pin's blast-radius justification named four consumers from architectural memory (outline, virtual docs, cell-background, crossref index) and every one was wrong — only two modules import the enumerator at all, and for these two languages the vdoc paths bail on an unmapped `cellLanguageId` before reaching it. The DESIGN survived all of it; only the CLAIMS were false — which is the point: a false justification passes every test, ships green, and misleads the next reader about what the tool actually does. | Whenever a fix ADDS suppression, or a comment/docstring states a universal negative about another tool's behaviour. Before writing "costs nothing" / "is never validated" / "renders exit 0": (1) enumerate the domain the claim quantifies (every key the feature can flag, not the ones you probed) and sweep it mechanically — 47 renders is minutes; (2) list the variables already known to change the verdict (document engine, comment char, case, fence token) and vary each one; (3) for any blast-radius claim, produce it as a GREP of who imports the symbol plus a reachability check, never as recollection; (4) if an exception survives, keep the design and state the exception with its measurement — an honest bounded claim beats a clean false one. |
| 176 | **When you SUPPRESS on another tool's say-so, the domain you must sweep is "everything the tool still rejects", and it is almost never the one mechanism you found the flag in — a suppression gate inherits every OTHER layer's validation as a lost true positive.** S163 taught the value-diagnostics feature to honour quarto's `validate-yaml: false` escape hatch. The gate was read straight from quarto's source (`context.format.render?.["validate-yaml"] !== false` around `validateDocument`), grounded across 58 documents, and the session correctly discovered on its own that the front-matter FORMAT NAME survives the flag (`format: banana` renders exit 1 regardless, because format RESOLUTION runs earlier) — and then wrote "THE ONE SURFACE the flag does not suppress is the format NAME" into three places. False. The exhaustive sweep the §9 review forced — all **170** top-level keys the feature can flag, one render each with the flag set — returned **26 survivors** (`toc`, `citeproc`, `ascii`, `incremental`, `columns`, `dpi`, `wrap`, `eol`, …), every one of which also fails without the flag, i.e. 26 real value errors the fix now silences. **The mechanism is the transferable part: they are rejected by PANDOC's Aeson decoder, a completely different layer from the quarto YAML-schema pass the flag gates.** The session had found ONE non-schema rejection layer (format resolution), generalised "so that's the exception", and never asked how many layers there are. A suppression gate does not suppress a mechanism — it suppresses a whole class of diagnostics, and every independent validator downstream of the gated one becomes a silent false negative. **Two corollaries, both measured.** (a) **The domain to sweep is what YOU can flag, not what the tool rejects** — the review swept "keys quarto rejects" and got a different, less useful number; the honest domain is `isWrongValue("banana", field) === true`, because a key the feature can never flag cannot cost a true positive (the S162 `layout` lesson, reapplied). (b) **A raw-token test against a PARSED-value gate is incomplete by construction.** The same session's `isValidationDisabledValue` compared the token to `false`/`False`/`FALSE` while quarto compares the parsed node, so anchored (`&a false`), tagged (`!!bool false`), aliased (`*a`) and next-line spellings all disarm quarto while we keep flagging — and the obvious repair is a trap: `!!str false` renders exit 1 while `!!bool "false"` renders exit 0, so a strip-the-tag-and-compare fix INVERTS the quoted-scalar rule it was built on. **Process note that mattered:** the session's own first anchor probe returned exit 1 and appeared to refute the review; it was wrong because shell double-quote escaping left a literal backslash in the YAML. Re-running with a heredoc reversed the result. A probe that contradicts a careful reviewer deserves a second look at the probe before the conclusion. | S163 §9 review (`wf_231f6a13-885`, 6 lenses, 42 agents, 2 refuters per finding, `agents_error:0`, ~2.58M subagent tokens; 18 findings surfaced, adjudicated firsthand — the false universal and two weak tests fixed in-session, the behavioural gaps filed with their sweeps). The 26-key exception and all four value spellings were re-measured by the session itself, and its own sweep was sharper than the review's. | Whenever a fix SUPPRESSES diagnostics on another tool's opt-out flag, feature detection, or version gate: (1) enumerate every INDEPENDENT validation layer the tool runs, not just the one the flag lives in — grep for other error sites, and expect at least one more than you found; (2) sweep the domain YOU can flag, mechanically, one probe per member, and report the survivors as a measured trade rather than an exception; (3) if the tool's gate tests a PARSED value, a raw-token matcher is incomplete on principle — enumerate the node-level spellings (anchor/alias/tag/multi-line) before claiming a spelling rule is complete; (4) when your own probe contradicts a reviewer, re-derive the probe (shell escaping, engine, format) before trusting your result over theirs. |
| 177 | **When you mirror another tool's decision, mirror its FILTER and then prove the mirror by running BOTH over the same domain — and when you assert what the other tool does, make sure the probe you measured it with is valid input to that tool.** S164 had to decide the schema scope of a cell option once the document engine is known. Reading quarto's `makeEngineSchema` showed the rule is one line (keep a `cell-*` field iff its `tags.engine` is absent, equals the engine, or is a LIST containing it) and that `SchemaIndex.cellOptions` already implemented that same filter — so the missing input was the engine NAME, not a new schema model. The proof then cost four lines: run quarto's rule and ours over all 43 fields the feature can actually flag, for all four engines, and set-diff. They agreed exactly — far stronger than the "only a knitr answer widens" written from a sample — and the same sweep surfaced the one genuine divergence (`engineTag` maps a multi-engine list to *agnostic*; quarto excludes such a field from the markdown/julia schemas), inert today only because the single such field is open-valued. **The second half is what cost this session most.** Three docstring claims about quarto's behaviour were false, and the worst rested on a probe that was not valid input: `{dot}` cells with `1 + 1` as the body, whose exit 1 came from a graphviz SYNTAX error and was written up as a structural chunk-option rejection. Re-measured with `digraph { a -> b }`, the claimed exit 1 was exit 0 and the real justification was a different key entirely. **Reusable rule:** a probe that fails for ANY reason proves nothing until you have read WHY it failed — an exit code is not a measurement, the error text is.
