| 178 | **When a fallback turns "we could not read it" into a CONFIDENT answer, every existing decline in the module silently becomes a claim — re-audit all of them before shipping the fallback, not after.** S165 taught the value-diagnostics feature quarto's default engine resolution (from the document's cell languages) so that `undefined` — previously "keep the per-cell language guess" — became reachable only in exotic cases. Every place the module already declined to resolve something (a node property, a block scalar, an alias, an empty token, a flow mapping, a front matter our scanner cannot see) had been written when declining was INERT: the caller fell back to the per-cell language, which was all it had anyway. After the fallback, those same declines resolved through the languages to a document-WIDE answer — knitr on any document holding an `{r}` cell — and so squiggled every OTHER cell of documents `quarto render` accepts. The §9 review measured **twelve** such shapes, all cardinal-sin false positives introduced by one line of intent ("an unresolved selector should not block the fallback"). The fix was one rule applied at every site: separate "we READ it and it names nothing" (quarto matched nothing either — follow it) from "we could not READ it" (quarto may have matched — block the fallback), which meant turning two booleans into three-way answers (`readEngineScalar`, `readTruthiness`). **The general form:** changing what a sentinel MEANS is a change to every producer of that sentinel, even though the diff touches none of them; grep every `return undefined` / `return false` in the module and ask what it now asserts. A second, cheaper tell: the docstrings that justified those declines (in three different files, including one the diff never opened) each contained a sentence of the form "declining returns us to the previous behaviour" — that sentence is the invariant the fallback breaks, so its presence anywhere in the module is the audit list. | Whenever a change makes a previously-inert default reachable as a real answer — adding a fallback, a resolver, a default branch, a coalescing operator over a value that used to mean "unknown". Before writing the fallback, enumerate the sentinel's producers and classify each as "definitely nothing" or "cannot tell"; only the first may feed the fallback. And run the end-to-end oracle against the PREVIOUS build as well as the new one: S165's own 48-document corpus reported "0 regressed" while twelve regressions sat outside it, and only replaying three builds (`git archive` + a `REPO` override) over the review-widened 64-document corpus turned that into a number. |
| 179 | **A verification harness that lives in a session scratchpad is not evidence — it is a claim; and the act of committing one is what exposes the drift it had already accumulated.** S164 and S165 each built an exit-code oracle (17 then 64 documents), each leaned on it for their strongest safety claim, and each left it in a disposable scratchpad — so "18 improved, 0 regressed" could never be re-checked by anyone afterwards, including by the next session touching the same code. S166's deliverable was simply to commit it, and porting it surfaced three defects that two sessions of heavy use had not: (a) **the mirror had silently drifted from the feature it mirrors.** `cellOptionFlags` re-walks `computeValueDiagnostics`'s loop because that function imports `vscode` and cannot be called headlessly — and S165's copy omitted the S163 `validate-yaml` escape hatch entirely. No corpus row used the flag, so the omission was invisible; a mutant deleting the guard (i.e. reproducing S165's version) now kills the new pins. **A copy of a decision needs a pin per step, or it is only a copy of the decision as it was on the day it was written.** (b) **the resource path was true on one machine** (`/Applications/quarto/...` hard-coded) where the product itself resolves it via `quarto --paths` through an already-tested pure function — a harness should reuse the product's resolvers, not re-derive them. (c) **the harness parsed quarto's schema with the CURRENT build's parser while replaying an OLD build's decision**, which is not a faithful replay; the parser must come from the build under test too. **The transferable rule:** when a piece of verification machinery is used twice, committing it is not tidying — it is the only way its own correctness gets reviewed, and its findings become reproducible rather than testimonial. **Two design points earned their keep immediately.** A committed BASELINE must require a written REASON for every row it records as wrong, because when the oracle fails the cheapest fix is to re-seed it, which silently promotes a new defect to "expected"; the gate was verified by deleting one reason and watching it name that row. And the comparison must NAME every regressed row and report rows present in only one build as *incomparable* rather than dropping them — silent omission is precisely how S165's own oracle reported "0 regressed" while twelve regressions sat outside its corpus. **Confirmation the port was faithful:** replaying `git archive 87b3f38` reproduced all three of S165's headline numbers independently — pre-S165 FP 16, shipping FP 4, 18 rows improved — which is the strongest available evidence that a re-implemented harness measures the same thing the original did. | S166 (committing the oracle). The three defects were found by porting, not by review; the escape-hatch gap is the one that would have produced wrong numbers. | Whenever a session builds throwaway measurement machinery and then relies on its output for a safety claim: budget the session AFTER it to commit the harness, and treat the port as an audit rather than a move. Pin every step of any decision the harness MIRRORS from production code (a mirror drifts silently and its output stays confident); reuse the product's own path/config resolvers instead of hard-coding what worked locally; make the build under test a parameter so any commit can be replayed; require a written reason for every accepted defect in the committed baseline; and name — never merely count — the rows that moved. |
| 180 | **A grep whose pattern cannot match its target returns the identical empty output to a grep that genuinely found nothing — so an inventory that publishes the empty result is presenting a measurement failure as evidence.** S167's plan was required (SESSION_RUNNER §Planning Sessions) to carry a grep-based evidence inventory, and it published `grep -n "diagnostics\[[0-9]\]\|\.at(\|sort(" test/integration/suite/yaml-value-diagnostics.test.ts` → no matches, concluding "the suite never asserts by array index". The suite names its array `diags`, not `diagnostics`, in all 11 declarations, so the pattern was structurally incapable of matching; six index-based assertions existed. The stated conclusion (diagnostic ORDER is unpinned) happened to survive, but only for a reason the plan never established — every one of those six sites is guarded by an `assert.strictEqual(diags.length, 1, …)` immediately above, and a one-element array has no ordering. This is the same defect class as Learnings #175/#176/#177 (a universal asserted from an unswept domain) with a new and more insidious mechanism: there, the sweep was too small; here, the sweep *silently did not run*, and its output was indistinguishable from success. The adversarial panel found it; the author did not. | Before publishing ANY negative grep result — "no matches", "no other call sites", "nothing references this" — first prove the pattern can match at all: run it against a form you KNOW returns hits (grep the bare identifier, drop the bracket, or grep a file you know contains the shape), and only then trust the empty result. Applies with double force inside a mandatory evidence inventory, where an empty result is read by the executor as a verified fact rather than an unrun command. Corollary for reviews: when a conclusion is right but the evidence offered for it is unsound, fix the evidence — a true conclusion resting on a broken measurement will be inherited by the next person who trusts the prose. |
| 181 | **An inventory grep is only as complete as the SYMBOL LIST you derived it from — and the safest source for that list is the deleted file's own exports, never the plan's prose.** Session 168's plan (itself panel-reviewed, and whose §11 headline was an unsound grep) told the executor to sweep for `oracle/flags\|cellOptionFlags\|OracleCoreApi\|oracle-flags` before deleting the mirror. Compounding it: `tsconfig.test.json` covers `test/oracle/**` and `test/integration/**` but not `test/unit/**`, so the dangling import was invisible to `check-types` AND `compile-tests` — the type error could only ever surface as a test failure. | Before deleting or renaming a module, build the grep's symbol list MECHANICALLY from the artefact itself — `git show <rev>:<path> \| grep -E '^export (async )?(function\|const\|interface\|type\|class)'` — and sweep each name, rather than trusting a list written in prose by an earlier session (including your own plan). Then re-run the FULL test matrix at that boundary, not the plan's per-layer subset: a per-layer gate list is an abbreviation, and anything it omits is structurally invisible at exactly the moment you are most likely to break it. |
| 182 | **A per-layer verification list in a plan is a floor, not the gate — following it literally can ship a red checkpoint commit.** The plan's Layer 3 stated its gates as `compile-tests` + `test:oracle`, and Session 168 ran exactly those and committed. That checkpoint (`c0d4fd2`) left `npm test` RED: Layer 3 removed `loadCoreApi` while a unit test still imported it, and neither stated gate could see `test/unit`. The breakage was found one layer later and its cause was then misattributed in the Layer 4 commit message to the *deletion* of the mirror files rather than to the *removal of the export* one commit earlier. Vertical-slice gate (c) says the complete build/test matrix runs at EACH layer boundary; a plan that lists a convenient subset per layer quietly overrides that, and the executor who follows the plan faithfully is the one who breaks it. | When executing a multi-layer plan, treat each layer's listed commands as ADDITIONS to the full matrix (`check-types`, `compile-tests`, `npm test`, plus whatever that layer names), never as a replacement for it — especially at a layer that removes or renames an export. When a breakage IS found late, trace it to the commit that introduced it before writing the cause into a message: the commit that surfaces a defect is usually not the commit that caused it. |
| 183 | **A citation is not evidence — when a docstring cites a prior finding to justify a hazard, re-read the cited lines, because the thing most often cited is the GUARD that already killed the hazard.** S169's new `document-engine-resolve.ts` opened with its load-bearing justification: passing `findFrontMatterValueLines` where `findFrontMatterTopLevelLines` belongs "type-checks and silently un-ships the container form (`document-engine.ts:38-45`)". Measured, that substitution is `error TS2345: Property 'hasChildren' is missing` — and `document-engine.ts:38-45`, the very citation, exists to record that `hasChildren` was MADE required for exactly this reason and closes with "Requiring the field turns that call into a compile error." I had read that block, taken the hazard from it, and not noticed it also reported the hazard fixed. The tell is grammatical: a citation supporting a present-tense hazard claim should be checked for past tense. **When to apply:** any time a comment justifies a design with "X would silently go wrong" and cites a source — open the source and check whether it describes the problem or the solution. A guard cited as a threat inverts the reader's model of what is protected. |
| 184 | **"Which cells does this change affect?" must be answered by enumerating the function's input space, not by naming the example that motivated the work — the motivating example is a sample, and a sample is not a direction.** S169 fixed completion scoping and described it, in three places, as fixing `{python}`/`{sql}` cells. A four-line table over (cell language × document engine) showed `{sql}` was never affected in that direction at all (`engineFor("sql")` is `undefined`, the UNFILTERED set, so `cache` was already offered) while `{ojs}`/`{js}` — never mentioned — were live instances, AND that two cells NARROW (`{sql}` in knitr, `{r}` in jupyter). The change was documented as a widening; it is both. The §9 review found the false half and, separately, that the `{ojs}` half was unpinned: a mutant excluding ojs re-opened the exact defect with all 1545 tests green. **When to apply:** before writing any prose that names which inputs a behavioural change affects, generate the full cross-product of the changed function's arguments and compute before/after for each. Cheap (one throwaway test printing a table) and it catches both the false claim and the missing pin, which are the same defect seen from two sides. |
| 185 | **A stated invariant can be true, precisely scoped, and still be the thing hiding the regression — check what it is silent about.** S169 claimed "the offered set is never a strict subset of the flagged set", which is true and was the point of the design: completion can no longer refuse a key the validator squiggles. But it compares completion to the VALIDATOR, not to what completion offered yesterday, so it is structurally incapable of noticing that two cell classes now offer FEWER keys than before. The invariant was not chosen to hide that — it was chosen before the narrowing was known — but it functioned as a reason not to look. **When to apply:** whenever a change ships behind an invariant, write down the question the invariant cannot answer and answer that separately. For a scoping change the two questions are "is it still safe?" (the invariant) and "did anyone lose anything?" (a before/after diff over the input space, Learning #184). |
| 186 | **Verify a mechanical multi-site edit by AUDITING the result, not by running the tests — a regex can land the right text in the wrong syntactic position and still produce a green suite.** S169 added a required third argument to 70 `completionContextAt(...)` call sites with one non-greedy `perl -0pi -e` substitution. The pattern's first `\)` matched the INNER `offsetAt(...)` call, so all 71 sites became `completionContextAt(text, offsetAt(text, 1, 5, () => undefined))` — argument in the wrong call, `completionContextAt` still receiving only two. It was caught by counting call shapes (`grep -o ... \| sed 's/offsetAt([^)]*)/OFFSET/' \| sort -u`), before any test ran. Tests would have caught this particular one (a missing thunk throws), but the near-miss is the lesson: the same regex applied to a site whose extra argument is merely *ignored* would have been invisible. **When to apply:** after any scripted edit across more than a handful of sites, enumerate the distinct resulting SHAPES and eyeball that set — it is a two-command check that does not depend on the tests being able to observe the mistake. |
| 187 | **A branch that DECLINES to answer is not neutral once the caller starts acting on answers — re-ask whether every historical decline is still the right one, especially the ones that were correct when written.** S164 made the `.Rmd` extension a VETO (`return undefined`) for an exactly right reason: an `engine:` key must not silence a document quarto validates anyway. The tell is in the S164 docstring itself: "What this deliberately does NOT do is scope those documents TO knitr" — a decline that documents its own incompleteness is a filed item, not a settled design. | When a module gains a new consumer, a new fallback, or a new confident-answer path, grep its own `return undefined` / early-decline branches and re-read each one's justification against the NEW caller. A decline written when the caller had nothing to lose becomes a claim the moment the caller acts on it. |
| 188 | **A verification corpus with a uniform input dimension cannot see a change keyed on that dimension — and it will report green rather than report nothing, which is worse.** Every one of the oracle's 66 documents was named `doc.qmd`. C1 therefore ran byte-identically green over the whole corpus — 59 agree / 3 lost TP / 4 cardinal FP, matching the predecessor's close-out figure to the row — while the branch it altered was untouched by every document in it. This is S165's horizon lesson recurring on a different axis: S165 missed twelve regressions on front-matter *shapes* outside its corpus; S170 would have missed the entire change on a *file name* dimension the corpus held constant. | Before believing a harness's verdict on a change, name the INPUT the change is keyed on and check the corpus actually varies it. Applies to any fixture-driven gate, not only this oracle: a constant is invisible precisely because nothing looks at it. |
| 189 | **A pin whose two operands agree by coincidence proves nothing, and the coincidence is easiest to introduce when the pin is about an OVERRIDE.** The pre-existing `.Rmd` pins were written to prove the extension is honoured — but they used `{r}`-cell documents, whose LANGUAGE fallback already answers knitr, so both the correct build and a build that ignored `fileName` entirely produced the same answer. The fix is mechanical: for a pin about input X, choose the other inputs so the answer WITHOUT X differs from the answer WITH it — here a `{python}`-only document, whose fallback is jupyter, so `"knitr"` can only have come from the extension. | Whenever pinning a rule that OVERRIDES or PRE-EMPTS another rule, construct the case so the two rules disagree. If the overridden rule would have produced the same answer, the pin measures nothing. Ask of every assertion: "what does the build that ignores this input return here?" — if it is the expected value, the pin is vacuous. (The project-specific form of the `pyDoc` habit S165's §9 review established, now shown to apply to the extension branch too.) |
| 190 | **When a widening's safety rests on a quantified claim ("all N of these are real"), the sweep is cheap and the reasoning is not — and the reasoning was measurably wrong once in this very session.** Adopting knitr on an `.Rmd` newly exposes 20 fields to being flagged, and the safety argument is that quarto rejects all 20. The measured split was **8 / 4**. Same session, same domain, same confidence, wrong by 60%. | For any change that widens what a tool reports, enumerate the newly-reachable set programmatically (a set-difference over the real schema, not a remembered list), then measure EVERY member against ground truth. Never publish a count, split or tally that was derived rather than observed — if a number appears in a docstring, a commit message or a ledger entry, it should be copy-pasted from a run. |
| 191 | **A filed item's measured DEFECT does not make its prescribed FIX measured — and a prescription, unlike a measurement, gets repeated verbatim across sessions without ever being re-tested.** The blank-line item was filed by S164 with the defect grounded firsthand (exit 0, with both controls), and in the same breath prescribed the fix: "closing it means teaching the scanner quarto's `trimLeft`". That clause was copied into `document-engine.ts` twice, restated by S165, and carried into S170's handoff as the ranked #1 recommendation — four sessions in which the defect's evidence lent unearned credibility to a fix nobody had probed. It was wrong. Quarto runs TWO partitioners and they disagree on purpose: `partitionYamlFrontMatter` (ENGINE) opens with `lines(markdown.trimLeft())`, while `validateDocumentFromSource` (front-matter VALUES) gates on `breakQuartoMd`'s first cell literally `startsWith("---")` — a byte-0 test with no trim. The actual fix — trim in `resolveDocumentEngine`, the one entry point both ENGINE consumers share — closes 5 with 0 regressions. **When to apply:** treat a filed item as two separate claims with two separate evidence bars. Before implementing the prescription, go to the upstream tool's SOURCE and check whether the surface you are about to change is the one the tool actually keys on; where a tool has two code paths over the same syntax, assume they diverge until measured. A defect verified firsthand is not a design verified firsthand. |

| 341 | **WHEN A PREDICATE IS KEYED ON A READER NAME, THE EXTENSION LIST OUTRANKS THE BASE — AND A NAME-BASED CLASSIFIER IS WRONG IN THE DELETING DIRECTION.** Session 205 measured this for `blank_before_header`; Session 209 measured it for two more constructs and found it holds identically. `gfm+definition_lists` renders a definition list and `markdown-definition_lists` does not; `commonmark+footnotes` renders a footnote and `gfm-footnotes` does not; and the two extensions are INDEPENDENT, since `markdown-footnotes` has definition lists and no footnotes, so one flag cannot express the pair. Each pin was therefore mutation-checked against a mutant chosen to express the axis it claims: `consecutiveBody === 1` → `>= 1` kills P1/P2/P5/P6; the column equality → CommonMark's `0-3` window kills P3; barring a thematic-break-shaped or indented line from being a TITLE kills P4/P5. Nine readers × eight markers = 72 documents, every one exit 0, produced a clean 6–3 split that is EXACTLY `FRONTMATTER_COMMONMARK_FROM` — the same set `atxClosingRun` already turns on, arrived at independently and therefore corroborating rather than assumed. When the split matches an existing flag EXACTLY, say so and reuse the flag; when it crosses that flag in both directions, you have found a SECOND axis and a second backlog item, not a harder version of the first. |
| 484 | **A CHARACTER CLASS IS NOT A PARSER, AND THE ROW THAT SEPARATES THEM IS CHEAP TO RENDER AND EASY NOT TO THINK OF.** The obvious spelling for "a long roman numeral" is `[ivxlcdm]{10,}`. It is measurably wrong: `ixixixixix.` is ten characters drawn entirely from that set and quarto renders a bare `<p>`, because pandoc's parser is ORDER-RESPECTING — it takes `ix` and then wants its delimiter. Transcribing the parser's own tier order (`m*(?:cm)?d?(?:cd)?c*(?:xc)?l?(?:xl)?x*(?:ix)?v?(?:iv)?i*`) predicts every rendered row the class gets wrong AND stays right on the invalid-but-parseable repetition runs the class gets right by luck. ⚠ Every tier is OPTIONAL, so the run matches the EMPTY string — without a length lookahead a line starting with a bare `.` becomes a list marker. | When implementing "is this token a NUMBER/NUMERAL/identifier in format X", find the upstream parser's actual acceptance order and transcribe it, rather than approximating with a character class. Then build the probe that SEPARATES the two spellings — for an ordered grammar it is a token whose characters are all legal but whose ORDER is not. And when a regex is an alternation of optional parts, ask what it does against the empty string before shipping it. |
| 485 | **SCORING EVERY LOSS CLASS AND A FIFTH OF THE GAIN CLASSES IS NOT A SCORE — IT IS A SIGN ERROR WITH A LARGE SAMPLE.** The first enumeration verdict on this change was 313 WORSE against 144 BETTER, apparently damning. Rendering all 1,587 classes reversed the sign — per class +132, per document +14,926. ⚠ The per-CLASS and per-DOCUMENT figures also disagreed at the intermediate build (−49 against +13,253), because the wrong classes are pathological and rare and the right ones are common. | Sample every category of a differential at the SAME rate, or render all of it; a per-category cap is a thumb on the scale even when each individual row is honest. Report both the per-class and the per-document score and reconcile them out loud when they disagree — the gap is the shape of the residual, not noise. |
| 486 | **A SURVIVING MUTANT USUALLY MEANS THE GUARD IS TOO WEAK, NOT THAT THE TERM IS REDUNDANT — BUILD THE GEOMETRY THAT REACHES IT BEFORE CONCLUDING EITHER.** Three of nine mutants survived the first hunt, two of them the reader gates this session had just argued were load-bearing. Removing all three gates in a candidate `src` copy and scoring it over 1,867 rendered documents found 6 rows where the ungated build DELETES a real heading — all in Session 198's 2/4/6 container-pop geometry, which no alphabet or design grid had contained. The one genuine survivor was then kept with a proof at its call site: its only reader is conjoined with a flag the capped grammar already makes false, so the two cannot disagree. | When a mutant survives, first ask what SHAPE reaches the term and build it — a candidate `src` copy with the term removed, scored over everything already rendered, localises it in one run. Only after that geometry comes back empty should you treat the term as unobservable, and then keep it only with a by-construction proof written at the call site (Learnings #445, and Sessions 246/248's own survivors). |
| 487 | **TWO CALL SITES OF ONE PREDICATE CAN ASK DIFFERENT QUESTIONS OF THE SAME BYTES, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM WANTS THE TRUTH.** Session 249's R4 named two functions ending in the identical character class `/^[ivxlcdm]+$/ || /^[IVXLCDM]+$/` and asked for the identical narrowing in both. The narrowing is right in `emptyItemMarkerIsPandocs` — 42,569 BETTER / 1,072 WORSE — and wrong in `popsEnclosingContainer` — 461 BETTER / 4,178 WORSE. The reason is structural, not tuning: the first asks what a line MEANS, where pandoc's parse is the whole answer; the second asks whether the marker CLOSES the container above, and that answer must mirror the PUSH `listItemContentColumn` performs on the same line. That push deliberately over-accepts `[a-zA-Z]{1,9}` (G4 pins `Elephants.` and `Dr.`), so the pop must over-accept with it; narrowing it alone strands the outer container's column and a later underline AT that column invents a heading. **When a filed item names two call sites, ask what each one's answer is FOR before assuming one change fits both — identical code is not identical intent.** |
| 488 | **BUILD THE DECLINED CHANGE AND SCORE IT; A DECLINE BACKED BY A NUMBER IS A RESULT, A DECLINE BACKED BY REASONING IS AN EXCUSE.** The pop half of R4 could have been declined in prose — the over-acceptance argument above is sound and was available before any measurement. It was instead built as a candidate `src` copy and scored over the 4,729 documents whose answer it moves, against 643 rendered witnesses. That produced the number that makes the decline auditable (461/4,178), the concrete witnesses for both directions, and the honest admission that the 461 are real heading DELETIONS being left in place. The re-filed backlog item is therefore actionable — it says the push and the pop must narrow TOGETHER — where a prose decline would have re-filed the same vague item the session started with. **Cost: one `cp -R src/core`, one candidate edit, one render batch.** |
| 489 | **AN ADVERSARIAL AGENT PROVING A PREDICATE HAS ZERO COVERAGE IS WORTH MORE THAN ONE FINDING A BUG.** A verification agent rebuilt the repo in a sandbox and mutated `popsEnclosingContainer`'s roman post-filter to `return true` and to `return false`: BOTH survived the entire 2,792-test suite. | 490 | **AN INSTRUMENT VALIDATED FOR ONE QUESTION IS NOT VALIDATED FOR THE NEXT ONE — AND THE INHERITED GRID IS THE EASIEST PLACE TO FORGET IT.** Session 249's `r5` geometry is a correct instrument for "does pandoc open a list here?", scored off the BLOCKS skeleton (`ul>ul>ol` against `ul>ul`), and its handoff said so plainly in gotcha 11. | 491 | **A CORPUS IS NAMED, NOT MEASURED, UNTIL YOU READ ITS DOCUMENTS — AND THIS PROJECT SWEPT A "CORPUS" OF ITS OWN PROBE OUTPUT FOR ~70 SESSIONS.** Every one of the 60,998 paths in `scratchpad/s249/corpusfiles.txt` lives under `scratchpad/` and is a prior session's generated probe; median document **51 bytes / 5 lines**. | 492 | **VALIDATE AN EXTRACTOR FOR THE PROPERTY YOU NEED, NOT THE ONE THAT IS EASY TO CHECK — "DOES IT FIND THE HEADINGS" IS NOT "DOES IT FIND ONLY THE HEADINGS".** `render250.sh`'s `H_DIRECT` column carries four documented extractor defects already fixed, and is still unsound the first time it meets an AUTHORED document: it requires heading text to contain no `<`, so `## A concrete \`SKILL.md\`` (a `<code>` span) scores as NO HEADING, and it simultaneously invents `Contents` and `Other Formats` from quarto's TOC and margin sidebar. | 493 | **CACHE THE EXPENSIVE ORACLE'S RAW OUTPUT, NOT JUST ITS EXTRACTION — THE EXTRACTOR WILL CHANGE AFTER THE RENDER IS DONE.** I rendered all 3,383 real documents, then found the extractor unsound, and had to re-render everything (25 minutes) because only the extracted headings had been kept. Adding a gzipped HTML cache cost 28 MB and made the next TWO extractor corrections free — seconds instead of a re-render. The cache also becomes the standing gate: the whole model-vs-quarto comparison is now a sub-minute re-run with no quarto invocation at all. | Session 251 (three extractor revisions, one avoidable full re-render) | Any harness that shells out to a slow oracle (quarto, a compiler, an LLM). | 494 | **A GENERATED CORPUS OVER-REPRESENTS EXACTLY WHAT ITS GENERATOR WAS ABOUT, AND THE BLIND SPOT IS SHAPED LIKE THE PROBE.** Measured across both corpora: the `from:` reader key appears in **7.9% of probes and 0.12% of authored documents** (4 files, 2 unique) — yet a large slice of the backlog is reader-dialect work. | 495 | **WHEN FANNING OUT, MAKE THE INSTRUMENT REFUSE TO PRODUCE THE DANGEROUS ANSWER, AND RE-RUN WHAT THE AGENTS REPORT.** This audit's dangerous direction is a false "enumeration-only" — it tells the operator an item is safe to ignore when it is not — and a BROKEN detector produces exactly that, indistinguishably from a true zero. So `scan.py` ABORTS rather than print a count when a detector fails its own `CONTROL`, every zero was re-attacked by a second agent forbidden the first agent's detector (**6 overturns**, each with a named document), and I re-ran all **147** detectors myself: **7 counts disagreed** with what the agents reported, moving **5 verdicts** — three of them DOWN from the more interesting verdict. | Session 251 (22 agents, 0 errors; the design put the refusal in the tool rather than in the instructions) | Any fan-out whose per-item output is a number you will aggregate. | 496 | **A LINE-NUMBER CITATION RESOLVES SILENTLY ONTO THE WRONG ITEM WHEN THE ROWS ARE EVENLY SPACED — AND THE "IS IT A VALID TARGET" GUARD CANNOT SEE IT.** Session 251's `final.json` keys each backlog item by its `BACKLOG.md` line number as of `b85626f3`; that same session then FILED a new item at line 52, so its own close-out `b50e5f6b` has every line below 52 shifted by +2. Items in that file sit exactly two lines apart (item, blank), so resolving a target against the post-filing commit maps item k onto **item k+1 — which is still a valid item start**. Of 90 targets, **83 resolved silently onto the wrong item** and only the 7 that happened to land on blank lines tripped the guard. The shape of the failure is the tell: a wholesale base-commit error should break EVERYTHING, so "only 7 of 90 failed" was evidence of silent success, not of a mostly-correct run. Two rules: state the BASE COMMIT beside the number when you record it, and verify the resolution against a NON-POSITIONAL property of the target (its title, its hash, its text). And when a guard fails on a strange fraction of cases, ask why that fraction rather than fixing the failures. |

| 500 | **A FENCE-AWARE GRAMMAR GIVES THREE DIFFERENT RECORD COUNTS AND NONE OF THEM LOOKS WRONG.** `HANDOFFS.md` reported **219** to `grep -c '^\`\`\`handoff'`, **216** to the trimmer, and held **218** real receipts. The real variable is the row's **last non-whitespace character** landing two or more columns past the border's right edge — trailing whitespace is stripped first and never fires — and there is a **second, independent trigger the report never mentions**: a `+===+` divider truncated at a column boundary. | 560 | **PANDOC'S ATX HEADING RULE IS COLUMN-EXACT EVERYWHERE, SO A CONTAINER NEEDS NO INDENT TOLERANCE OF ITS OWN.** Inside a grid-table cell `|### x` (no space) and `| ### x` (one) both render a heading and `|  ### x` (two) renders literal text — which looks like a table quirk and is not. At top level with no table present, ` ### x` at one, two or three spaces renders `<p>### x</p>` and four renders a code block: byte-for-byte the same boundary. Pandoc strips the cell delimiter plus **at most one** padding space and then requires column 0, exactly as `ATX_HEADING`'s docstring already records for the document body (Session 199 removed the CommonMark ` {0,3}` class for this reason). ⚠ A container fix that "tolerates 1–3 spaces because CommonMark does" manufactures phantoms at every indent ≥ 1, not just at 4. |

This is #561 one step further: not merely that a failing document is invisible, but that **an improvement can be an artefact of that invisibility**. The score summarises the documents that render; the bundle diff is the only instrument that sees the rest. For any change reaching `findHeadings`, read the diff's document count and its quarto-exit column FIRST and the score line second — `tools/realdoc-score/run.sh <label> <dir>` scores any directory holding `src/`, so the comparison costs one extra run over a throwaway copy. |

Re-run without the pipe, twice: `exit=1 input=DELETED html=no`, deterministic. Use `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`, or redirect to a file and test the status directly — and treat any exit code read through a pipe as unmeasured. ⚠ **AND THE SAME SESSION SHOWS THE MIRROR-IMAGE FAILURE, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF: a NON-REPRODUCTION MEASURES YOUR PROBE, NOT THE CLAIM.** Two agents reported that `quarto render s.qmd` deletes a neighbouring `s.rmarkdown`; I re-ran it, `s.rmarkdown` survived, and I recorded "does not reproduce" in `BACKLOG.md`. It does reproduce — my `s.qmd` held **no code chunk**, so knitr never ran, and it is the knitr path that claims `<stem>.rmarkdown` as its own intermediate and deletes it. With a chunk: exit 0, `s.html` written, `s.rmarkdown` gone (a same-stem `s.md` survives, so the collateral is extension-specific). A refutation needs the same standard of construction as the claim: before writing "does not reproduce", name what differs between your probe and theirs. Two agents agreeing is still one hypothesis stated twice — but one negative probe is also just one probe. |

| 572 | **A GRAMMAR IS NOT A PIPELINE — WHEN THE FIX IS "THE ENGINE'S OWN GRAMMAR", INTERSECT IT WITH WHAT THE NEXT STAGE ACCEPTS.** R5's mechanism is that knitr consumes a chunk before pandoc sees it, so the obvious predicate is knitr's own `chunk.begin` class, `[a-zA-Z0-9_]+`, read straight out of R. Shipping that verbatim would have manufactured **5 phantom headings**: knitr's rewrite target is a pandoc CLASS, and pandoc refuses a class that does not begin with a letter, so a digit-led or `_`-led engine name runs away anyway one stage later — and the model was already right there. Measured, `quarto pandoc -f markdown -t html` with `<pre>` present as the discriminator: `.zzz9` `.x2` `.x_` `.cpp11` `.glue_sql` open, `.2x` `._x` `.99` `.9zzz` are refused; confirmed end to end with executing `quarto render` on `.Rmd`. The shipped predicate is `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*` — knitr's grammar **∩** pandoc's class grammar — with both tables in the docstring so the next session does not "simplify" it back. | Whenever a fix models one stage of a multi-stage pipeline. Transcribing stage N's grammar is necessary and not sufficient: stage N's OUTPUT must also survive stage N+1. Ask "what does the stage I am modelling hand to the next one, and does that survive?" and measure the handoff, not just the entry. |

The probe had no trailing bare fence, so a REFUSED opener's closer was absorbed into the paragraph instead of starting a runaway, and the heading survived either way. The discriminator for "did the fence open?" is `<pre>`, not the heading downstream of it. One look at the raw HTML showed `<p>```{.2x .cell-code} a</p>` and settled it. | Any time a probe's PASS and FAIL states are distinguished by a downstream effect. Grep for the thing you are actually testing, not for its consequence — and when a result says "everything behaves the same", print one raw output before believing it. The operator caught it with a question. |

A check can be the bug: my first before/after comparison used `sed 1,0d` (which drops line 1 of ONE side only) and reported `model.tsv DIFFERS`; `cmp` and `shasum` on the whole files said identical. When a verification disagrees with the expectation, suspect the probe first (Learning #691). |

| 696 | **A GRAMMAR INFERRED FROM A HANDFUL OF PROBES IS A GUESS: WHEN THE ALPHABET IS SMALL, RENDER ALL OF IT.** Session 303's first knitr header reader refused "any empty slot" (three probes). The grid became a closed-world fixture, `test/fixtures/knitr-header-shapes/quarto-1.7.33.json` (245 rows: header, then the ids quarto defined), and one test reads every row: no phantom, no loss except a named, reasoned list. | 697 | **A HUNT EARNS ITS COST WHEN THE AUTHORS ONLY WRITE AND THE PARENT RENDERS: 200 DOCUMENTS FOUND 25 NEW PHANTOMS THAT 150 PROBES AND 45 MUTANTS HAD NOT.** Four authoring lenses (grammar, containers, engines, interplay) wrote 50 documents each and were forbidden to render; the parent rendered all 200 in about 4 minutes at 3 wide and scored the new reader against quarto. | 698 | **R'S `$` PARTIAL-MATCHES NAMES, AND AN UNQUOTED TOKEN IN AN R-PARSED SLOT IS CODE.** Two knitr facts a reader gets wrong until it measures them (Session 303, quarto 1.7.33). `labelx=` and `label.x=` are matched to `label` by R, and both ids end undefined, while `LABEL=`, `Label=`, `lab=` and `my.label=` are ordinary options. A bare token in any slot but the first is parsed as R and written back, so `label=fig-x-007` defines `fig-x-7`, `1e3` becomes `1000` and `100000` becomes `1e+05`; the first slot (knitr quotes it itself) and any quoted string are the text as written. A reader that accepts "anything shaped like an id" invents labels in both cases. | 704 | **A TEXT READER'S BLIND SPOTS BECOME THE RULE'S: EVERY SPELLING THE ENGINE RESOLVER CANNOT SEE FLIPS AN ANSWER.** The resolver reads front matter as text, so each YAML spelling it misses makes quarto run one engine while the index assumes the other, and a rule that depends on the engine then removes a label (60 rendered documents of round 2, 20 of round 3): a flow mapping, an anchor or complex key, one space of indent, a quoted container key, an escape, an apostrophe inside a flow list, `jupyter: ""`, a no-break space at the end of a value (the resolver trims it with JS `\s`, YAML keeps it), an opener led by a space, a value continued on the next line, a metadata block lower in the document, a BOM, an unterminated block. | 705 | **THE TWO ENGINES PUT THE CROSS-REFERENCE ID IN DIFFERENT PLACES, AND THAT DECIDES EVERY RULE (QUARTO 1.7.33, MEASURED).** knitr puts a FIGURE's id on the output and a TABLE's on the cell, so `eval: false` or `output: false` or an empty chunk kills a figure label and leaves a table's, while `include: false` kills both. Jupyter puts both ids on the cell, so `eval: false` alone and `output: false` alone keep the label (the code is still on show) and only a cell with NOTHING left to show is dropped: `include: false`, an empty source, `echo: false` with `eval: false` or `output: false` or a comment-only body. `keep-hidden: true` re-shows what include, output and echo hide, so every rule built on those is wrong with it on. | 706 | **AN EQUIVALENT MUTANT IS DEAD CODE: DELETE THE CLAUSE, AND REBUILD THE MUTANT LIST AFTER EVERY REFACTOR.** Three clauses of the closer test (its length, a same-line closer, `startsWith(indent)`) survived 7 of 7 mutations because the scanner already guarantees them; they were replaced by one anchored regex and the mutants re-aimed at it. | 707 | **A RULE MUST NEVER BREAK THE INDEX: TIME THE PATHOLOGICAL INPUT, SEPARATE YOUR COST FROM THE PARENT'S, AND CATCH WHAT A READER CANNOT FINISH.** Three of my own defects were found by timing hunter documents in node rather than by reading: a regular expression built from a document's indent threw `Invalid regular expression` at a 200,000-space indent; two lazy `(.*?) *$` patterns cost 5 s on a 40,000-space run and 12 s on 64,000; and an existing option reader overflowed its stack on a 12 MB header string that the parent never reached.
